TalkText:
TREASURY PORTFOLIO

In Attendance

Senator Ayres, Minister for Industry and Innovation, Minister for Science

Reserve Bank of Australia

Ms Michele Bullock, Governor

Dr Christopher Kent, Assistant Governor, Financial Markets

Productivity Commission

Ms Danielle Wood, Chair

Professor Alex Robson, Deputy Chair

Dr Lisa Studdert, Head of Office

Dr Stephen King, Commissioner

Ms Rosalyn Bell, First Assistant Commissioner

Mr Barry Sterland, Commissioner

Committee met at 09:00

CHAIR ( Senator Darmanin ): Good morning, everyone. I declare open this hearing of the Economics Legislation Committee into the 2025-26 supplementary budget estimates. I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today and pay my respects to their elders past and present. I extend that respect to all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people here today. The committee has set 17 October 2025 as the date by which senators are to submit written questions on notice and 28 November 2025 as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice for today's proceedings. The committee's proceedings today will begin with the Reserve Bank of Australia. The committee will be conducting today's hearings via video conference and in person.

Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session. This includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that in giving evidence to the committee they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee. Such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence.

The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance for questions at Senate estimates hearings. Any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of Senate estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise. The Senate has resolved that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted.

Witnesses are reminded of the Senate order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised. I incorporate the public interest immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

(Extract, Senate Standing Orders)

CHAIR: An officer called to answer a question for the first time should state their full name and the capacity in which they appear. I also remind all senators that, as we continue our work implementing the Set the standard report, as chair I will ensure that proceedings are conducted in an orderly, respectful and courteous way.

Reserve Bank of Australia

[09:03]

CHAIR: Welcome, Ms Bullock and Assistant Governor Kent. It's over to you for an opening statement.

Ms Bullock : I won't make an opening statement.

CHAIR: Thank you very much. I will kick off with the first couple of questions. We have seen inflation moderate significantly from its peak in 2022. Can you talk a bit about what has moderated inflation and perhaps make some comments on whether it has been broad based amongst a range of categories, such as goods and services or other areas? What does this mean for the moderation in a number of measures of inflation, please?

Ms Bullock : Sure. If you go back to when the inflation was at its highest, back at the end of 2022, when it hit 7.8 per cent, there were a couple of factors involved in there. The first is that this was around the world. Inflation had risen substantially around the world. There was a big supply chain issue associated with that. You might recall during the pandemic there were logistics issues. There was particular trouble with getting goods to where they needed to be around the world. That was creating supply chain issues. At the same time, there was energy price rises. The Russian invasion of Ukraine resulted in substantial increases in energy. There were these supply side issues. There was also a sense in which demand was really strong. Around the world, again, and in Australia, governments had responded to the pandemic by increasing fiscal spending, which was appropriate. Interest rates had dropped around the world to practically zero, so there was a massive demand side impact. What happens when supply chain issues meet strong demand? We ended up with strong inflation.

Since then, it has come down. It has been for a couple of reasons. The first is supply chain issues have resolved themselves. Energy prices are still high but they are not increasing at the same rate they were. For many other goods, which were in short supply, their prices have stopped rising and, in some cases, declined a little. At the same time, interest rates had risen. They had moved from very accommodative levels to restrictive levels. That has dampened demand in the economy. That is also what has contributed to the decline in inflation.

So it has been broad based. It has been broad based across both goods and services, although I would have to say that in Australia, like many other countries overseas, services inflation does remain a little sticky. It is higher. It has been offset by slightly lower goods inflation. Services inflation is still up around three per cent, and in some countries it's a bit higher than that. So it's generally broad based. There is a bit of difference, as there always is, in different components of inflation. But we target total inflation. We don't target individual components of it. At the moment, we're in a situation where we've got inflation back in the band at the moment. The key now is to make sure it stays there sustainably.

CHAIR: Thank you. In terms of our labour market performance over the period, how would you say that the state of our labour market compares to the historical performance of the labour market over a longer period of time?

Ms Bullock : I think if you had said to us that we could have an unemployment rate with a four in front of it sustainably—if you had said that back pre COVID—I think people would have been a little bit sceptical, or some people would have been a bit sceptical. What we have seen is that with the post-COVID low, if you like, of 3½ per cent unemployment, at that point all the indicators were that the labour market was extremely tight. When you've got a very tight labour market, that can put upward pressure on inflation. Since then, we've seen the unemployment rate rise to about 4.2 per cent. I emphasise, though, that during that period employment has continued to grow. It's not that jobs are being lost. It's just that employment is growing. It's just not growing as quickly as the labour force is growing. So we have seen the labour market now ease. We still think it's possibly a bit tight, particularly in some areas, but we think that's a bit uncertain. It could be close to balance as well. There's a bit of debate about that. We're open to those discussions. Certainly at the moment I would say the labour market is in a pretty good place. The forward looking indicators look reasonably stable. We're expecting the unemployment rate to drift a bit higher over the rest of the year. At the moment, I think the labour market is in a pretty good place.

CHAIR: Notwithstanding your comments just then about perhaps what you might expect in terms of the labour market, I think what you are saying more broadly is that inflation has moderated. It has certainly gone down. The labour market has remained resilient. Wages are growing. We heard this yesterday from the Treasury secretary as well. In terms of what this means for growth in real incomes, what would you say are the factors that are driving real income growth?

Ms Bullock : So at the moment what is driving real income growth is that wages are still rising. Inflation has come down. If you are talking about real disposable income, then interest rates have declined a bit as well. That is putting money back in people's pockets. There has been some tax relief as well. If you look back to what was driving the decline in real wages back a couple of years ago, you see that inflation was really a very important part of it and tax was another part of it. Interest rates were part of it as well, but tax and inflation were the really big components. As those things have reversed direction, we are now seeing growth in real wages. In fact, real per capita wages are now above what they were pre COVID. So they've recovered that.

CHAIR: Overall, that's a pretty good story.

Ms Bullock : Yes.

CHAIR: I will finish and then hand to my colleagues. In terms of, I guess, the return of real income growth, could you talk perhaps finally about what it means for the economic recovery that we have seen? We heard a bit about this yesterday from the Treasury secretary. From your perspective, which sector has been the key driver of growth in our economy? If you could highlight a couple of areas, that would be helpful.

Ms Bullock : For some time we have been expecting that as real incomes start to recover, consumption will start to recover. While real incomes were falling, obviously that wasn't good for households and consumers. They weren't inclined to consume. We are starting to see that consumption is starting to recover now. That reflects the growth in real incomes. It also reflects a wealth effect. As people are observing housing prices rise, perhaps they are watching the equity markets and they are feeling a bit more wealthy. That also tends to result in people consuming a bit more. What we've started to observe in the last little while, in the previous year probably, is that a lot of strength was coming from government. What we're starting to see now is a bit of a switch between the public and the private sector. The last national accounts certainly demonstrated that the private sector and private demand was starting to now drive growth. We're expecting that to continue.

CHAIR: Thank you.

Senator PATERSON: I have some questions arising out of the most recent monetary policy board statement. You also just alluded to the issue in your last answer. I will quote the statement. You said:

Data for the June quarter show that private demand is recovering a little more rapidly than expected, taking over from public demand as the driver of growth.

I'm firstly interested in the second part of that statement—taking over from public demand as the driver of growth. Could you unpack that for me? It's fair to say, isn't it, that public demand has been largely the driver of growth up until recently?

Ms Bullock : So it has been true up until the end of last year, I think, probably, that for the past couple of years household consumption, which is a big driver of private demand, has been very weak. We discussed some of the reasons for that. Real incomes had been declining. People weren't feeling confident. Interestingly, people had jobs, but interest rates were rising and had remained high. All of these sorts of things were playing into that. During that period, public demand was in fact filling that gap that consumption and investment wasn't filling. What we've seen more recently is public demand ease. As we've discussed, with all those other factors, we are seeing consumption recover at the same time. We are seeing a swing in how the private sector, as we've described it, has taken over from the public sector as driving some of the growth.

Senator PATERSON: I want to come to that aspect of the statement in a moment. Firstly, I want to dwell for a moment on the public demand driving growth for the last couple of years. It's interesting to me that you describe very strong public demand filling the gap, perhaps. It has also come at a time when we've had, I think, one of the tightest tightening cycles in history. Is that right? Is there any more rapid period of tightening?

Ms Bullock : No. Probably interest rates rose most rapidly than they ever have. I think it was the most—

Dr Kent : But from the lowest point.

Ms Bullock : From the lowest point, from practically zero. So you do need to emphasise that we were coming from zero.

Senator PATERSON: Indeed. Good point. As you say, that tightening cycle is one of the things that has contributed to the weakness of private consumption. Obviously households have been squeezed by rising interest rates. It seems slightly incongruous to me, then, that you've got rapidly growing or fast public demand, a rapidly tightening cycle of interest rates and weak private demand. It seems to me that suggests public demand was contributing to the need for increasing interest rates in that period.

Ms Bullock : I've talked a bit about this before. Obviously, we don't control fiscal policy. We control monetary policy. We take fiscal policy as given. What fiscal policy was doing, I think, in that period—they were doing it during COVID as well—is trying to support the economy through what was a pretty bad period, quite frankly. At the same time, just aside from that, the public sector has to provide services and infrastructure to the Australian economy. They've got to balance all these different demands on their purse. So what they do with that is their decisions and the government's decisions. We take it as given. What would have happened if public sector demand didn't fill that gap? Would interest rates have been lower? I don't know. They might have been. It's also true that you might have ended up with much lower employment and other impacts on the economy. So my observation would be that where we find ourselves now is that the private sector is starting to recover and growth in the public sector is starting to ease off. We've got a good unemployment rate so far. We've got inflation back in the band. We're in a pretty good spot.

Senator PATERSON: Surely, though, as a matter of simple economics, all else being equal, had public demand been softer, interest rates could have been lower. We can't say with confidence how much lower, but there are only a few components that make up demand. Had one of those been softer, it would have had implications for interest rates and inflation.

Ms Bullock : It might have. It also might have been that interest rates had to be lower because the economy was actually much softer and doing much less well and employment doing much less well. I can't tell you the counterfactual.

Senator PATERSON: That's fair. I can't hold you to the statements of your predecessor. But your predecessor has publicly said that government spending made his job harder during this period.

Ms Bullock : I don't recall Phil saying that. He has possibly said it. I don't know.

Dr Kent : Possibly going the other way.

Senator PATERSON: Pardon?

Dr Kent : Possibly going the other way.

Senator PATERSON: What do you mean by that?

Dr Kent : Prior to the pandemic, we were trying to generate—

Ms Bullock : Yes. That's true

Dr Kent : more wage growth and inflation and encouraging spending, particularly in infrastructure.

Ms Bullock : The government was basically cutting back on government spending. That might have been what he was referring to—governments.

Senator PATERSON: Let me tell you exactly what he said. I am quoting from an article in the Australian Financial Review on 19 August this year headlined 'Labor's spending made RBA's job harder: Lowe':

Former Reserve Bank of Australia governor Philip Lowe says the federal government has no budget discipline and its "cost-of-living" spending on households made it harder for the central bank to fight inflation.

That's the AFR's summary. I will go to his direct quotes:

After COVID, we haven't really got back to a clearly articulated framework for decision-making with fiscal policy," Lowe said in frank remarks released on the first day of the government's economic reform roundtable in Canberra. …"

Those frameworks are really important in disciplining the political process. It seems to be 'where there is a need we'll spend'."

He goes on in the article. I want to make sure I'm being accurate in quoting him.

Ms Bullock : Well, certainly Phil, though, is free to say what he likes. I'm not going to comment on what he said.

Senator PATERSON: Fair enough. As I said, I can't hold you to the observations of your predecessor. But he was the governor during this period when interest rates were increasing. He has said that the government made his task harder by spending too much. I will come back to the other aspect of your statement that private demand is taking over from public demand. Can you unpack for me the June quarter national accounts and help me identify why you believe that private demand is taking over from public demand?

Ms Bullock : Well, consumption was stronger than we had expected during that period. There were some things to do with energy rebates and so on. Nevertheless, it was stronger than we had been expecting. Having said that, we had been expecting it to pick up. As I said earlier, real incomes have been picking up. Wealth has been rising. Those things generally result in—

Senator PATERSON: And rates have come down.

Ms Bullock : And rates have come down. Basically, those things generally result in an increase in consumption. Consumption is a really large chunk of private demand. That's what is sort of driving it. We would be expecting it. It's starting to show up in the June quarter. It's a bit more than expected. Some of these things can jump around a bit. Nevertheless, it's going in the direction we thought it should.

Senator PATERSON: I will go to the specific numbers in the June quarter. I had it here that growth in household consumption was 0.9 per cent. Does that sound right to you?

Ms Bullock : Yes. That sounds right.

Senator PATERSON: Dr Kent is nodding as well. Growth in government consumption was one per cent. Government consumption was still stronger than household consumption. Is that right?

Ms Bullock : Well, it's much of a muchness.

Dr Kent : The other point is that it's a much smaller share of the economy, so the contribution to GDP growth, particularly over the year, for government has definitely come down and private has come up. Yes, you could focus just on the June quarter. I think our statement is as much about the trends over a number of quarters.

Senator PATERSON: I accept that. But we have certainly not reached that crossover point where household consumption is growing faster than government consumption, have we?

Ms Bullock : No. But that is to Dr Kent's point. Because consumption is a much larger component of GDP, it is taking over as the stronger driver. That's the point.

Senator PATERSON: The monetary policy board statement does point to June quarter data specifically. It doesn't talk about the trend over time. Maybe that's what it was referring to. It says that data for the June quarter shows that private demand is recovering a little more rapidly than expected and taking over from public demand as the driver of growth. Has it really taken over that yet, or is it just on a trend to?

Ms Bullock : I think it's looking to. The June quarter data suggests that. We do not say that one quarter therefore makes a trend. We don't say that. Again, as I've said, this is something you would expect to be happening given what else we're seeing happening with real incomes. So we have been expecting this. This is part of the process of lower interest rates, rising real incomes, lower inflation and a reasonably strong labour market.

Senator PATERSON: Obviously the other part of demand is investment. I understand that the June quarter figures for private investment is 0.1 per cent. Does that accord with your numbers?

Ms Bullock : Are you talking about a year ended number or a quarterly number?

Senator PATERSON: Good question. That is what I'm told on the numbers I've got in front of me. I think they are the quarterly figures.

Ms Bullock : Business investment, if you think about it over the past year, has been reasonably solid. It has been—

Senator PATERSON: For clarity, I'm talking about private investment. I think business investment is one component of private investment. Again, correct me if I am wrong. You will know better than me.

Ms Bullock : Well, ask the question and then we'll—

Senator PATERSON: Thank you. In the June quarter, public investment was down 6.7 per cent. Obviously that's a lumpy figure. We're talking—

Ms Bullock : That's volatile and lumpy, yes.

Senator PATERSON: Growth of private investment was 0.1 per cent. As I understand it, the component of business investment is even more flat than that. That doesn't indicate roaring good health, does it?

Ms Bullock : Well, again, it's a quarterly number. I would make the same point with consumption. It's a quarterly number. You can't read ups and downs. Business investment, private investment, has been actually not doing badly. If you take mining out, it hasn't been doing too badly on some things. Software, for example, has been doing quite well. Data centres have been doing quite well. There are some components of investment that are doing fine.

Senator PATERSON: I guess I'm trying to understand your level of confidence about private consumption replacing public demand. We've heard across Treasury and Finance estimates this week that real government spending growth was 5.5 per cent last year. Real growth in the economy was 1.4 per cent. In the last financial year, public spending is growing at four times the rate of the economy. That doesn't sound to me like the step change handover. Let's see what happens in this financial year. Maybe decisions of government will alter that. The trajectory we seem to be on is still for very strong public demand and reasonably modest private demand.

Ms Bullock : Well, again, I think you've got to come back to the point about contributions. The contribution of the private side of things is actually starting to increase. I think that's what we're talking about. We're starting to see that shift. I think the contributions are telling you the story.

Senator PATERSON: But if federal government spending continued on that trajectory—obviously, state governments are a component; I haven't tallied all their numbers—it wouldn't be a handover from public demand to private demand. It would be kind of continuing strong public sector demand at that rate, wouldn't it?

Ms Bullock : Well, I can't say what's going to happen with public demand in the future. We just take whatever Treasury have for their forecasts. With our current forecasts and using their current forecasts, we continue to see private demand picking up over the next year and starting to take over from public.

Dr Kent : Our GDP growth forecast is around two per cent over the next year and a bit. Most of that is from private demand.

Senator PATERSON: I hope we can sustain it.

Dr Kent : There's still a quantum from public, and that's federal and state.

Senator PATERSON: I hope we get to that. Chair, I have questions on a different topic, if you want to rotate the call.

CHAIR: Yes.Let's rotate. Senator McKim.

Senator McKIM: Good morning to you both. Thanks for coming in. The RBA's latest financial stability review noted your concerns about the rush of investors back into the housing market and that could cause a rapid upswing of house prices. You articulated some concerns around its impact on financial stability. Could you talk to the committee a bit about that, please, Ms Bullock? Specifically I note your comments from your press conference, I think it was, about a week ago—late September, in any event—where you spoke about supply and the lag in supply. I'm not trying to quote you here; I'm just paraphrasing. You'll use your own words, as you should. Could you talk a bit about the situation we find ourselves in in the property market? You expressed at that press conference that you think it's a difficult situation. For what it's worth, I think many millions of Australians would agree with you at the very least that it's a difficult situation. Could you just talk about, firstly, your financial stability review and your concerns there about the impact of a rush of investors back into the housing market and what some of the responses to that might be? Secondly, more broadly, could you talk about how we find ourselves in this, as you've said, very difficult situation and what some ways out of it might be?

Ms Bullock : I wouldn't say we expressed substantial concern about investors coming back into the housing market. The issue on the financial stability side about investors we were trying to highlight is that what investors can do is exacerbate the cycle in the housing market. In the past, there have been concerns that as investors exacerbate the cycle in the housing market, it results in people borrowing too much, loan-to-valuation ratios tending to rise and high debt to income ratios and that introduces vulnerabilities into the system. That's the concern. We don't see it manifesting at the moment in a severe way. Certainly we don't see loan-to-valuation ratios and high debt to income ratios and those sorts of loans rising very substantially. We don't see that at the moment, so that's positive. All we're highlighting is that it needs to be kept an eye on because it can aggravate these cycles.

On the broader issue about the housing market, it's true—and I've said this a number of times—that the issue with the housing market is supply and demand. We have demand for housing that outstrips the supply of housing. It's occurring both in housing prices and rents. There's more demand for rental properties than there are rental properties available. I think this is where it gets a bit complicated. It's true that on the one hand investors buy houses. But then they rent them out to people. In Australia, the rental stock—many countries don't have this—is effectively owned by other household investors. You've got a situation where people want to rent. They've got to rent from someone. They rent from investors.

The question is: if there were fewer investors, might there be more houses that people could buy? You would still have a need for renting, so who is going to provide the rental stock? So it's a complicated situation. I would say that at the moment what we're observing with investors is typically what we observe in these cycles. Investors are the first ones to pick up.

Senator McKIM: Thanks. I have a few questions off the back of that. Firstly, we are seeing housing investors getting back into the market, are we not? Growth in lending for housing investors accelerated to 6.6 per cent in the year to August. That's up from 3.9 per cent a year earlier. Do you accept that we are seeing more housing investors or property speculators entering the housing market? Can you confirm that would put upward pressure on prices?

Ms Bullock : I think I already said, Senator, that, yes, what we usually expect when interest rates decline and you see a recovery in the housing market is that the investors tend to respond first.

Senator McKIM: And we are seeing that currently?

Ms Bullock : We are seeing that. Do you want to comment on credit?

Dr Kent : No. That does sound about right.

Senator McKIM: You've said, obviously accurately, Ms Bullock, that there are supply and demand factors at work here. I note your comments that you made about supply and the delays that inevitably are going to exist in terms of building more housing supply. When you said it was unusual—I don't want to misquote you here—the amount of property that is, I guess, owned by other households for investment, are you referring to the fact that we don't have a large stock of publicly owned housing in Australia?

Ms Bullock : No. Not necessarily public. For example, there's a lot of build to rent in other countries. It's not just public housing. Corporations and pension funds own housing; it's that sort of thing. There's a different mix in Australia.

Senator McKIM: Thanks. I understand that you deal with a lot of other things, but interest rates are within your purview. You have been very happy to talk about supply. Are there any other levers the government could pull to limit the attractiveness of existing housing as a speculative asset?

Ms Bullock : No. I don't have any particular policy views on that. The bottom line, as I've said, is that we've got to get the supply of housing moving. My observation, certainly living in New South Wales, is that the governments are trying really hard to get this moving. That involves planning. It involves construction. It's a whole series of things that governments are looking at. I encourage them to keep looking at it.

Senator McKIM: You have been very clear, though, that is going to take some time.

Ms Bullock : Well, it does take time. It takes time to get approvals. One of the big things is higher density housing. That by its nature takes much longer. It is not something where you can just turn the switch and say, 'Right, now we're off and running.' It takes time.

Senator McKIM: Are you aware of the play Waiting for Godot by Samuel Beckett?

Ms Bullock : I am aware of that, yes.

Senator McKIM: A play where famously a critic said it's a play where nothing happens twice because it's in two acts. Are we just going to wait for supply? Is that it? That's what you would say to basically most of an entire generation of Australians who are priced out of the housing market at the moment—you've just got to wait for supply to catch up and there's nothing else that government can do? Is that your view?

Ms Bullock : I'm not going to suggest government policies. Government runs government policies on housing. The policy that I've got control over is the interest rate. Supply is the genesis. There might be some other things governments can do. That's up to them. Really supply is the big thing here. It has been a structural issue for many years. It didn't just start in the last year or so. It has been an issue for a number of years.

Senator McKIM: It certainly has.

CHAIR: You are at eight minutes.

Senator McKIM: Are you doing 10-minute blocks?

CHAIR: Yes.

Senator McKIM: Thanks. Ms Bullock, you mentioned LVR as the source of risk, didn't you?

Ms Bullock : It can be a source of risk. The reason it can be a source of risk is higher loan-to-valuation ratios. If someone defaults, the reason it's a potential risk for the financial institution is that there is a greater possibility that the collateral might not cover the loan. That's why we think of it as a slightly greater risk to the financial institution.

Senator McKIM: Thank you. Therefore, does the ability for people to now take out a 95 per cent loan-to-valuation ratio increase that risk?

Ms Bullock : Not for the financial institution, no. If you are referring to the government guarantee over the deposit, no, because it's guaranteed. The financial institution is not at further risk.

Senator McKIM: Would reducing or abolishing the capital gains tax discount reduce demand and, therefore, prices, or at least reduce the growth in house prices?

Ms Bullock : I have done no particular analysis of what the removal of the capital gains tax might do, Senator.

Senator McKIM: I guess, Ms Bullock, you're very happy to talk about supply. That's fair. Why won't you talk about demand and some of the levers that the government has at its disposal to address demand?

Ms Bullock : It's a very easy thing to talk about supply and demand. It's a much harder thing and requires much more analysis to talk about the plethora. It's not just one policy. There's a plethora of policies. I have not done an analysis of those various policies to decide whether or not different policies would have different impacts and what you should do with them holistically. That's not my bailiwick.

Senator McKIM: But financial stability is an area of concern of yours?

Ms Bullock : Yes.

Senator McKIM: If you're concerned about financial stability and you've indicated that you're concerned about house prices, if you are concerned about those two things, why wouldn't you do an analysis of some of the levers that are available to government and start jawboning on things like the capital gains tax discount, which is the most inequitable tax concession on the books by a long way in Australia? Why wouldn't you start talking about those things? Jawboning about that would help focus the public debate on some of the things the government might be able to do to reduce demand and, therefore, address your concerns about house prices, intergenerational equity and the stability of our financial system.

Ms Bullock : I don't think, Senator, it's my job to tell the government what they should do with their policies. My job is to look at what the impact on financial stability might mean and then to think about ways that we might address that through macroprudential policies, for example, working with APRA.

Senator McKIM: Does the RBA—

CHAIR: I have to rotate the call.

Senator McKIM: This is my last question, Chair, thank you. Does the RBA accept its share of responsibility for how high property prices are in Australia? Dr Lowe, your predecessor, effectively said that the quantitative easing that you engaged in in the early pandemic period was too aggressive. I'm paraphrasing him here. The RBA printed $400 billion-odd in the early year or two of COVID and effectively handed it over to retail banks, who then turned around and lent it into the property market. Do you accept that played a role in the housing price bubble that we've seen over the last five years in Australia?

Ms Bullock : Certainly part of the way monetary policy works is through the housing market. But I would not accept that the Reserve Bank is responsible for the housing price issues in this country.

Senator McKIM: You don't accept that you played any role whatsoever in the housing price spike of the last five years?

Ms Bullock : As I said, what happens with monetary policy as part of the transmission mechanism is through the housing market. We know that. Again, the problem is the lack of supply relative to demand. When monetary policy eases and housing demand picks up, supply can't pick up as quickly. That's where you end up. It's not monetary policy's responsibility to look after housing prices.

CHAIR: Thank you.

Senator PATERSON: Governor, I want to ask you some questions about the recent monthly inflation prints. I preface that by saying that I have heard you say many times that we need to be cautious about the monthly figures, that they are variable and that the RBA puts greater stock in the quarterly figures. Nonetheless, the two most recent monthly prints have been higher than were expected. There has been a very strong reaction from economists, who used very strong language to describe last month's indicators particularly. They called it a shocker and used other language like that. There is also a market response, changing the expected time for the next rate cut from 100 per cent probability in November, which is probably a bit too confident now, to less than 50 per cent. What do you think has been driving the increased or higher than expected inflation in those last two monthly prints?

Ms Bullock : Caution, again. You've got to be a bit careful because monthly data are quite volatile. It depends on whether you're looking at headline or the trimmed mean. The headline jumped up, but there were some things going on with the timing of energy rebates and so on. That's why we tend to focus on underlying. The other caution I would make is that the trimmed mean in a monthly sense is not the same as the trimmed mean in a quarterly sense. So you can't just read into the trimmed mean for monthly what it might mean for the quarterly. Having said that, there were two components. We get a reasonably good read from the first two months of these monthly indicators on a couple of things—housing and services. Both dwelling costs inflation—that's the cost of building new homes—was a little higher than we had been expecting and inflation in services was a little higher than we had been expecting. That's made us think that when the September quarterly comes out there is an upside risk to our forecasts in those because those things are looking a little higher than we thought they would be.

Senator PATERSON: That quarterly data is out in late October, isn't it, I think days before your next—

Ms Bullock : The week before our next board meeting.

Senator PATERSON: board meeting, yes. Obviously, that will be more indicative. What does this indicate more broadly about the fight against inflation? Is this just, in your view, the last mile challenge and it's just that last sticky bit to be defeated? Is there a risk that actually the fight against inflation is going to be a more enduring, ongoing one and that we have to be much more guarded about the upside risks here?

Ms Bullock : We'll do some more forecasts for our November meeting. At the moment, we think the risks are relatively balanced on both sides. We had been expecting inflation for this last bit to be slower to decline. It came down very sharply and then it has been a much slower, gradual decline. We had expected that. As I said earlier, we're in a position where we think the labour markets may be still a little bit tight or may be close to balanced, depending on who you talk to. It's possible that we've got a situation where growth is starting to pick up at the same time as inflation is just back in the band and employment is being maintained. In those cases, there might be some upside risk. It's also possible, though, that what we saw in the June quarter with respect to consumption isn't maintained. You've got all of this uncertainty, which I think the Treasury talked about yesterday. You've still got all that uncertainty out there with the international environment—China and the United States. So you've got balance on both sides. That's why the board says it's trying to be data driven; it's trying not to pre-empt. It's trying to think about the risks. It's trying to use the data as the data come in to inform where it thinks things will be going in the next six months or so. So that's why we do need to make sure that we remain data driven.

Senator PATERSON: You mentioned energy rebates as part of the reason for the volatility in the monthly figures. I think certainly in the July quarter there was a very obvious case. I think there was a New South Wales state government payment, which was paid two days before the month or two days after or something, which had an impact on the data. But it's also true that, as you say, part of the big falls in inflation last year were driven by those energy rebates, weren't they?

Ms Bullock : Well, no. Some of the initial big falls from the peak weren't driven by that.

Senator PATERSON: Trimmed or headline? I thought they had a big impact on headline.

Ms Bullock : Well, with headline coming down from 7.8 per cent, a lot of that was just across the board.

Senator PATERSON: Oh, sure. I'm not disputing that.

Ms Bullock : So the last year or so, energy rebates have contributed. I think the numbers are 0.2 per cent. I think that is the amount that we've seen come off. So it's not massive. It's not like one or two percentage points. It's fractions of a percentage point. So we will be giving that back when the rebates come off. So you might get an uplift then.

Senator PATERSON: Which is this calendar year. Those rebates are all starting to come in.

Ms Bullock : Well, the rebates at state government level have been coming off. That's why you're seeing some of the inflation numbers go off as those come off. But the Commonwealth's have been extended to the end of the year. So that will continue to subtract about 0.2 per cent from inflation. When they come off, that will get given back.

Senator PATERSON: You also mentioned the labour market. Obviously there were the ANZ figures out last week, which are softer than people were expecting. How much stock do you put in that?

Ms Bullock : Again, it's just one indicator. We look at a range of indicators across the labour market. I would say that the forward looking indicators are vacancies and job ads. Notwithstanding that, they wiggle, but they've been reasonably stable over the past six months or so. It's one month's figure. Broadly, it has been stable. But it is something that we look at.

Senator PATERSON: The other data out recently was the Westpac data on consumer confidence, which took a big hit. Do you attribute that to the public's changed expectations about the interest rate pathway?

Ms Bullock : I don't think that the consumer confidence numbers have really recovered. I don't think we've seen them pop up as interest rates declined—

Senator PATERSON: No.

Ms Bullock : and then start coming off again. Consumer confidence has remained quite low. I don't think we have a really good explanation for why. Certainly as we talked about earlier, we are seeing people start to consume again. They are consuming discretionary goods and services, not just essential ones. So there's a bit of a puzzle about what might be going on with consumer confidence.

Dr Kent : And it's not unique to us in Australia. It's a global phenomenon.

Senator PATERSON: I agree with you that generally it has been low. But even from that low level it fell even further. The Westpac-Melbourne Institute index declined by 3½ per cent from September to October. That's a material decline. Any thoughts on the driver of that, if not interest rate expectations?

Ms Bullock : No. I wouldn't say so. As Chris just said, around the world we're seeing low consumer confidence, even as interest rates are declining here. Even as we're observing that people are responding by consuming discretionary goods and services, their confidence is still low. It's a bit of a conundrum. We don't really know why that is.

CHAIR: Senator Roberts.

Senator ROBERTS: I have circulated a graph from the Australian Bureau of Statistics. Ms Bullock, I certainly appreciate your direct and concise answers. I think you have talked quite a bit about how the RBA is looking through the energy bill subsidies and impact on headline inflation. What are you seeing in the underlying increases in the price of electricity? As I show in that graph, it has increased 23 per cent in two years. That seems like an incredible shock to the economy. How do you think about that? What is the impact of your management of inflation?

Ms Bullock : So there are two aspects to that. What you will see from this graph that you have pointed out is that it rises in June 2023. That was the delayed energy price shock that many other countries saw following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Basically, then, it's a new price level. The price level has risen, but you haven't seen inflation because the level has just been the same.

Senator ROBERTS: Flat?

Ms Bullock : So there is a step up in the level. There has been a more recent increase, as we've seen the default market offers rates come out. Basically, the way we would think about it is that, in a direct sense, if you've got a supply shock, you've got a new price level. That doesn't necessarily lead to ongoing inflation and an impact on inflationary expectations. We can afford to say that's a level shift and we will look through it. The extent to which it has indirect impacts through cost impacts on businesses, that's where we would watch to see that it wasn't feeding through into consistent and persistent inflation. So far, it doesn't seem to be driving persistent inflation, the increase in the price level for energy.

Senator ROBERTS: What are your thoughts about when the energy bill relief stops?

Ms Bullock : Well, the energy bill relief, obviously, is government policy. They put it in place to address the cost of living. Your graph shows why—because energy prices rose quite a lot. It has moved the inflation figures around quite a bit. As I've discussed in many other contexts, we've therefore looked at the underlying inflation to get an idea of the underlying pulse of inflation. That is what we have been focusing on in order to base our interest rate decisions.

Senator ROBERTS: We saw the government's economic roundtable was supposedly focused on productivity. What do rising energy costs do to productivity? What is the impact, then, on the standard of living?

Ms Bullock : I don't know if there's a very direct impact of rising energy costs on productivity. There's a much more fundamental thing about productivity, and that's dynamism in the economy and dynamism among businesses. What we have been observing for decades is that productivity growth has been declining not only here but overseas. To some extent, at least, the evidence suggests that lack of dynamism in business is part of the reason for that.

Senator ROBERTS: So the underlying inflation on the electricity index is at 23 per cent. Including subsidies, it has been brought back to seven per cent. Many consumers still have about a 16 per cent increase to catch up with. What will that do to inflation numbers in the future?

Ms Bullock : Well, headline inflation, as you'll see from our forecasts, will rise as the energy rebates come off. But the more important thing is what is happening to the underlying pulse of inflation. We are continuing to see that decline.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you. I understand that household inflation expectations have a big impact on inflation itself. At the economic roundtable, Treasurer Chalmers said:

Real wages are growing at their strongest rate in five years, inflation has a two in front of it and interest rates have been cut three times in the last six months.

People are still talking about high grocery bills and inflation in insurance premiums and all kinds of insurance. What does that do to people's expectations of inflation?

Ms Bullock : Well, all the evidence we have is that inflationary expectations have remained reasonably anchored at around 2½ per cent. That's what has made it possible, I think, to bring inflation back down toward the target range so that we're now under three per cent and heading towards 2½ per cent and to maintain a relatively healthy labour market. You couldn't achieve that without anchored inflation expectations.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you. I have a quick question before I go to a separate topic. What does having 4.5 million visa holders, non-citizens, in the country do to demand for houses and to the price of houses?

Ms Bullock : Well, certainly the more population you have, the more demand for housing you have.

Senator ROBERTS: It has been six months since the new board arrangements started. How is that working so far?

Ms Bullock : I think it is working well. The monetary policy board now has more time to focus on monetary policy decisions. The governance board, I think, is adding significant value in helping me. I was the sole accountable authority for the institution. Now the governance board is the accountable authority. My own view is that the people on that board are adding significant value.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you. Is there going to be a review of these changes?

Ms Bullock : The governance board is going to do a report, I think, by the end of the year. It is going to talk about all of the recommendations from the review, where we're at with meeting them and what our plans are to meet those that we haven't yet.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you. You actually have three boards—the monetary board, the governance board and the payment system board. Have there been any developments coming from the work the Reserve Bank is doing on electronic payment systems, whether that's some form of central bank digital currency, which I think your predecessor acknowledged was done, or a unified digital currency the banks have been talking about? Is anything happening there in either the domestic market or international settlements?

Ms Bullock : A few things. We have done some experimentation. Back in 2023—we might have talked about this before—we did a pilot of a central bank digital currency. We asked people to come with use cases and so on. The main headline out of that was that the predominant use cases were not what I would call retail CBDCs. It wasn't about putting central bank digital currencies in the hands of you and me and using them at shops. It wasn't about that. It was about wholesale digital currencies—how you can potentially use central bank digital currencies in markets for wholesale assets. We've got another experiment going on now which is looking specifically at that issue. If you tokenise assets—you put them on a chain, a ledger—how can you use not only central bank digital currencies but stable coins, tokenised bank deposits and standard payment systems to settle tokenised asset sales. That is the current experiment that is going on. We are working with a number of organisations to do that. That will give us a bit more information about the sorts of issues that might arise in moving towards tokenised asset ledgers.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you. During COVID, the Reserve Bank pursued a policy which had the effect of creating money through electronic journal entries and using that to buy securitised mortgages from Australian banks. How many securitised mortgages originating in the Australian property market is the Reserve Bank now holding?

Dr Kent : We have to take this on notice. I suspect it's close to none. We don't accept them as part of our regular operations. Most of them we would have held would have been a result of the term funding facility, which has now rolled off and completed.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you. I don't think you've had this question directly. Are you worried about housing prices? Is there a risk in the property market which may be factoring into policy planning?

Ms Bullock : The focus that we have as an institution on that, as I said earlier, is potential financial stability implications and what fast rising property prices might do to the rise in risky lending associated with that. That is our angle on that.

CHAIR: Senator Roberts, you're almost at time.

Senator ROBERTS: I have just two more questions, Chair. During COVID, the Reserve Bank printed $608 billion. I think it is called quantitative easing. This made a significant contribution to the recent inflation spike. The government is projecting deficits across the forward estimates. Having mind to your inflation target, is there any capacity to fund these deficits by quantitative easing rather than through borrowing?

Ms Bullock : We don't fund government borrowing. The government has to borrow to meet its obligations. The Reserve Bank basically uses the interest rate to influence inflation through our impact on demand. What we observe is that inflation is now back in the band.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you. Do you have a figure for how much more the government can borrow? Are we getting into a danger zone with all this borrowing for inflation, the exchange rate, credit ratings and such like?

Ms Bullock : No. I don't have a figure for that.

Senator ROBERTS: This is my last question. We have the highest real estate prices in the world. If we had more cities, I'm sure they would be in the top 10 in the world as well. As it is, our top five cities are in the top 10 of the world. What is that doing to inflation and to the standard of living?

Ms Bullock : Well, housing inflation finds its way into inflation figures through two things—rents and the cost of building houses, if you like. So they are in inflation there. Housing prices themselves don't find their way into inflation. We don't target housing prices.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you very much.

CHAIR: Senator Sharma.

Senator SHARMA: I have some questions about the RBA's review of merchant card payment costs and surcharging. What is the timeline for the implementation of those proposed changes?

Ms Bullock : We put a consultation document out; I think it was in July. We are now in the process of looking at 170-odd submissions, some with quite extensive detail in them, and meeting with many of those people face to face. I myself have had a number of meetings with them. The plan is to take something back to the November payment system board which summarises where we've got to with consultation. At that meeting, the board will decide what the next steps will be.

Senator SHARMA: I think I've seen a proposed effective date of 1 July 2026. That was in the consultation paper.

Ms Bullock : That was for surcharging, yes. We'll have to look at that. When we've analysed all the submissions and we've got the consultation done, the board can have a look at that.

Senator SHARMA: I noticed in your paper you make the claim that the current system involves cross-subsidisation of larger merchants by smaller merchants. Can you just explain that judgement.

Ms Bullock : So the way the card payment systems work is that there is a thing called an interchange fee. It's set by, effectively, the schemes. It is paid by the merchant's bank, if you like, to the issuer. Big merchants usually get a deal that says they will pay interchange and they will pay a small amount over the top of that.

Senator SHARMA: And smaller merchants aren't able to negotiate that?

Ms Bullock : Smaller merchants basically get told, 'You will pay one per cent or 1½ per cent.' We've done a lot of work on this. We've put a lot of articles out on it. You can show that the smaller merchants pay much higher merchant service fees than the large merchants.

Senator SHARMA: I saw a figure in there as well. You estimate that, I think, 10 per cent of small merchants actually pass the surcharge on to customers. How did you derive that figure? Anecdotally and non-empirically, it feels a lot higher to me when I go to small merchants.

Ms Bullock : Well, I think it feels higher to people because it's salient merchants. It's merchants that you go to to get your cup of coffee from every day. I think that's why people sort of think many more surcharge. I'd have to take the question on notice. I think the answer is that we get it from the acquiring businesses. So they can tell us, I think. Can I come back to you on that?

Senator SHARMA: Yes. Take that on notice. It's 10 per cent by number of merchants rather than by volume of transactions done by—

Ms Bullock : Yes. And, if it were volume of transactions, I suspect it would be smaller because, of course, none of the really big merchants surcharge.

Senator SHARMA: The proposal, as I understand it, is for the RBA to revoke its prohibition on no-surcharge rules—

Ms Bullock : Correct.

Senator SHARMA: which would then allow the card issuers and banks to—

Ms Bullock : The schemes.

Senator SHARMA: The schemes, rather?

Ms Bullock : The schemes to reimpose their rules for—

Senator SHARMA: Their no-surcharge rules—what if they don't, because that's at their discretion?

Ms Bullock : Well, if they don't, we don't feel that we have the powers to ban surcharging. If the government felt they wanted to, then that would be in their hands. I would have to say that, in any jurisdiction where they're allowed to impose no-surcharge rules, they do.

Senator SHARMA: So your expectation would be that they impose it?

Ms Bullock : My expectation is that they will. I would have to say that the schemes are very supportive of removing the ban on those surcharges.

Senator SHARMA: The basis of this change benefiting smaller businesses in particular, as I understand it from your consultation paper, is that the RBA will cap interchange fees—I think I'm using the right terminology here—and that those lower fees will be passed through to small businesses. Again, what level of confidence do you have that the lower interchange fees will feed through to small businesses?

Ms Bullock : Well, we would hope that competition would lead to that. There are quite a number of acquirers out there, not only banks but also non-banks that do acquiring. It's also true, I think, that we're alert to the fact that it might not pass through as it should. We would certainly be relying on competition to do it. But, if it doesn't—I think my colleague Brad made this point at the House of Representatives committee the other day—we have got other things we could do if it looks like it's not being passed through.

Senator SHARMA: I don't think I heard your colleague at the House committee. Would you mind elaborating a little on what you could do if they are not passed through?

Ms Bullock : Well, we have other powers. We could perhaps look to cap merchants under—we have some new powers coming through at the end of the year. We might be able to do some things there. The other thing we're going to do is make it more transparent. Small merchants often don't understand. They're looking for simplicity. They don't understand what their options might be. If we can force some more transparency onto it so that small merchants can see, 'I'm paying this, but I could pay that over there' that might help. There are other things we can do which might assist.

Senator SHARMA: I see. What's your expectation of what this will mean for consumers? If this reform is implemented in full and plays out as you expect, consumers will no longer be paying surcharges. Will they be paying higher prices? Will any of this—

Ms Bullock : This is potentially a very long answer. The card payment system, as an ecosystem, has a number of costs associated with it holistically. We can argue at the edges about what those costs should incorporate. Let's assume that we all agree on that. The question then is about how those costs are distributed and who pays them. On one reading, you could say, 'Well, we just charge the merchants a whole lot of money and then we use that to subsidise everyone else.' If the merchants can't surcharge, yes, it will go into their prices, just like other costs of their business do.

I think it's really a question about distribution. Someone is paying. It's just a matter of how they are paying. If it finds its way into merchants' costs and ultimately into their prices, all the consumers pay. If you allow surcharging, arguably it doesn't, and some consumers pay and others don't. Again, my point would be here that we're really talking about distribution. We're not talking about somehow reducing the amount that overall has to be paid. The costs have to be met.

Senator SHARMA: From what I understand from your modelling, though, it is the domestic issuers under this package that take the biggest haircut, for want of a better term, in terms of how the costs are distributed?

Ms Bullock : If interchange fees are capped at lower levels, yes, there's less revenue for domestic issuers, yes. They have to make that back elsewhere if they feel they need to. That's right.

Senator SHARMA: I notice, I think it was even in your paper or your testimony before the House economics committee, the analysis that generous credit card reward schemes are currently being cross-subsidised by debit cards and less generous credit card reward schemes. Is that roughly how it works? Everyone is paying the same surcharge fee, but some cardholders are getting quite generous benefits and others are not.

Ms Bullock : Yes. Think about the way loyalty schemes work. They are an incentive for people to use a credit card. That's what they are. Credit cards cost more to accept than debit cards. At the moment, what we're seeing with the surcharging regime is that is not reflected in the costs facing consumers. They face the same surcharge or no surcharge at all to use a credit card as a debit card. The incentives are skewed towards using a credit card.

Senator SHARMA: Okay. How will this scheme operate or not with three-party schemes such as Amex and digital wallet schemes? Will it have any impact on how people pay at the moment?

Ms Bullock : At the moment, we can't regulate them. Our new powers will allow us to regulate three-party schemes.

Senator SHARMA: Would the intent be to—is that something you examined?

Ms Bullock : Our intent would be to be looking at where, to the extent that we are regulating the four-party schemes, that might be creating an unlevel playing field with the three-party schemes. We'd be looking at that.

Senator SHARMA: I notice from your paper references to the UK experience in capping interchange fees and how that's played out. Have you also been looking at the Canadian and New Zealand models?

Ms Bullock : We have been looking at all those models. What I should point out is that we were the first jurisdiction to cap interchange fees. Everyone else followed us. Some of them have gone further than us. We are now looking at their experiences, having gone further than us, and what things fell out and whether there are lessons for us. Yes, we are.

Senator SHARMA: Thank you. They are all my questions.

CHAIR: Senator Bragg.

Senator BRAGG: I want to ask you some questions about housing, Governor. My understanding of your evidence is that the major issue in the Australian housing market today is one of supply being deficient. Is that right?

Ms Bullock : Yes. As I've said a number of times, we've got demand for housing, and supply isn't able to meet it.

Senator BRAGG: Are you aware broadly that the government in Canberra has significant supply policies? It has significant programs, such as the Housing Australia Future Fund, housing targets and other schemes. You're aware of these schemes, I imagine.

Ms Bullock : Yes. I'm aware of those schemes.

Senator BRAGG: The government has been in power for over three years. You said after the recent interest rate judgement:

I'm not confident that it's going to make any impact in the next two years.

That was your comment in relation to the supply side. Why don't you think any change can be achieved on the supply side in two years?

Ms Bullock : When I said that, my answer was that it takes up to two years really to get any momentum on approvals and construction and so on. What we're talking about here is high density. That stuff doesn't happen overnight. I wouldn't take the two years as being precise—that exactly in 25 months we're going to have a boom in housing. I don't mean that. What I mean is that basically it takes time for approvals and building. We know at the moment, actually, that construction is slow.

Senator BRAGG: I want to ask you about the demand side. Have you been asked by the government to do any analysis on the changes to the Home Guarantee Scheme, the five per cent deposit?

Ms Bullock : No.

Senator BRAGG: Have you done any analysis internally on what it might mean for prudential stability?

Ms Bullock : No. We haven't. We've looked at other people's estimates of what it might mean for housing prices—that seems to vary between very little and six or seven per cent—but we've done none ourselves.

Senator BRAGG: What do you think it will do to house prices in the short term?

Ms Bullock : In the short term, it's possible that housing prices might be a bit higher than they otherwise were.

Senator BRAGG: Right. Do you think it will be a short-term impact or medium term?

Ms Bullock : Well, it depends, again, on how supply responds. We are seeing a lot of movement in supply. Certainly in New South Wales—there's a lot of movement there.

Senator BRAGG: Sure. When you say 'higher'—what sense do you think?

Ms Bullock : I've done no analysis of how much higher housing prices will be in response to this, no.

Senator BRAGG: Has the bank done any analysis on that?

Ms Bullock : No.

Senator BRAGG: Is that something that you could take on notice?

Ms Bullock : Well, there's no need to take on notice whether or not we've done any independent analysis of it. We haven't. If you're asking whether we will do work on it, it'd have to figure in our priorities. I'm not sure that specifically at the moment is one of our priorities.

Senator BRAGG: I understand that this is a matter for APRA as the prudential regulator. They have to make judgements about these things. But you do also have a whole-of-economy role and mandate. Lending policy, as we've discussed in the past, partly does have some relevance to the RBA, doesn't it?

Ms Bullock : It does. That's why we do have a great deal of dialogue with APRA. One of the recommendations of the review was that we put our macroprudential work with them on a much firmer footing, which we're doing.

Senator BRAGG: Even the Treasury has said that there will be higher prices. Some of the market economists have said that there could be five or six per cent. Some have said it could be as much as 10 per cent increases. Are we talking here about entry level prices or entry level first homes?

Ms Bullock : Yes. I'm unsure what the question is. Yes.

Senator BRAGG: There's potentially a price impact. I'm not seeking to verbal you. You said in your own words you haven't done the analysis. You said before that it's possible there could be higher prices. The other factor here, of course, is that there will be people with much higher loan values. There will be higher LVR arrangements, won't there?

Ms Bullock : Yes.

Senator BRAGG: Do you have any thoughts on more people having higher LVRs in the community?

Ms Bullock : Well, they just have to be aware that, under this policy, instead of having lenders mortgage insurance—they basically have the backing of the government—they still have a much higher loan-to-valuation ratio. That means that if they do find themselves in difficulty—hopefully they don't—with the collateral value underlying that, there's a risk that may not cover the loan. If housing prices decline, when you have a high loan-to-valuation ratio, it doesn't take as long or as much for housing prices to decline and you're in negative equity. That's the main outcome of having a high loan-to-valuation rate.

Dr Kent : The other point to make, of course, is that borrowers in such a situation will face higher repayment costs. They will take that into account when they are deciding how much to borrow and whether to get in with a small deposit or wait a bit of time.

Senator BRAGG: They are the two risks to individuals. Those are the two major risks to individuals. Is that right?

Ms Bullock : Well, the risk to individuals in the sense that they've got to meet their higher loan repayments. It's possible that they may not be able to recover the cost of the loan if housing prices decline and they need to sell. Ultimately, that's a risk for the banks.

Senator O'NEILL: But that risk is mitigated.

Senator BRAGG: How is it mitigated?

Dr Kent : The government guarantee.

Senator O'NEILL: Well, there was the answer to questions from Senator McKim just a little while ago.

Ms Bullock : The government guarantee—what happened before was that there was lenders mortgage insurance to give the financial institutions comfort that if something happened, they would still get their money back. Now the government is filling that.

Senator HUME: I have some follow-up questions from Senator Paterson specifically about inflationary expectations, which I know you and I have spoken about before. Ms Bullock : Short-term inflation expectations can spike according to a number of things. In fact, when inflation was quite high back in 2022, we did see short-term inflation expectations rise. That was logical because people were observing everything that they were buying going up in price quite substantially. There are what we sometimes refer to as salient prices. Fuel is one of them. People focus on that. There are, I think, some grocery prices that people tend to focus on. These sorts of things can make short-term increases and decreases in inflation expectations.

What's more important, though, is that over the medium term, over the longer run, inflationary expectations remain anchored. That is important because that is what factors into merchants' decisions and businesses' decisions about their own prices and factors into wage expectations for consumers. So, if inflation expectations rise, consumers start to think, 'Well, I need more wage rises and larger wage rises in order to compensate me for that.' Businesses say: 'Well, wages are rising by that. I see generally prices are rising. I can raise my prices by three or four per cent because everyone else is raising their prices by three or four per cent.'

Senator HUME: So it becomes a self-perpetuating prophecy?

Ms Bullock : The whole thing becomes self-perpetuating. The way that I like to describe it is that if inflation—which it was prior to COVID—is low, relatively stable and in the background, and people aren't thinking about it, then it doesn't get embedded into all of these sorts of decisions. CHAIR: The committee will commence with the Department of Industry, Science and Resources corporate enabling and business services. I remind senators and witnesses that the committee has set 17 October 2025 as the date by which senators are to submit written questions on notice and 28 November 2025 as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice. The committee welcomes senator the Hon. Tim Ayres in his capacity as Minister for Industry and Innovation and Minister for Science. I also welcome Ms Meghan Quinn, secretary of the Department of Industry, Science and Resources. Minister, do you have an opening statement? You said earlier that perhaps you would?

Senator Ayres: Yes. Reluctantly, I can see that maybe I should say a few things at the outset. It won't be my normal practice. I'm inclined to try to get to questions as quickly as we can. Given it is the first run through this, I thought I would make a few observations at the beginning. Of course, the decade leading up to 2035 is consequential for Australia's security, our economic prosperity, our competitiveness and our productivity. Effective industry policy is crucial to Australia meeting the key national challenges in economic resilience and security and growth and productivity and building good jobs in Australia's regions and suburbs.

Industry policy that works in the interests of Australia and Australians depends upon strong alignment and partnership between the public and private sectors across Australia's research, technology and innovation systems. It also depends upon the Commonwealth's economic, skills training, resources and climate and energy strategies. This includes at all levels of government, particularly state and territory administrations. Crucially, it also requires close coordination across the department's industry investment, science and innovation functions and the resources portfolio led by my colleague Minister Madeleine King.

Australian industry faces real challenges too. There have been several decades of deindustrialisation, particularly in the automotive sector, where the loss of tens of thousands of engineers, designers, tradespeople and manufacturing managers has hurt our capacity to grow new industry. There is overcapacity in international markets, unfair trade practices and subsidises. These mean our manufacturers are not on a level playing field. We have the double challenges and opportunities of energy shifts with global industrial decarbonisation and investment in new capability. Finally, as our partners and competitors focus and move on industry policy, we need to ensure that Australia develops a modern, fit-for-purpose industrial and investment strategy that meets Australia's immediate and long-term national interest.

I've worked hard on the foundations laid during the first term of the Albanese government, which has the largest pro-manufacturing agenda in Australian history. We are reforming our anti-dumping arrangements, consolidating all of Australia's trade remedies that were historically shared between the Productivity Commission and the Anti-Dumping Commission into the Anti-Dumping Commission. We are issuing the ADC with a new statement of expectations that lifts its ambition and purpose. We are providing additional budget support to ensure our anti-dumping regime is modern and fit for purpose in a tougher world.

We are also taking a disciplined approach and on a shared basis with state governments to deal with industrial challenges in heavy industry and metal smelting across Australia. Colleagues would have seen a support package for Nyrstar's Hobart and Port Pirie zinc and lead smelters developed jointly with Tasmania and South Australia. I was in last Queensland this week to announce the successful conclusion of negotiations with Glencore over the future of the Mount Isa copper smelter. It will protect copper smelting, refining and mining capabilities and vital phosphate processing capabilities. It lays the foundations for future resources and industrial jobs and investment and supports the many thousands of North Queensland blue collar jobs that rely upon those facilities.

We are continuing to work on the Whyalla steel intervention in the interests of our industrial and steel capabilities. Building on the establishment of the National Reconstruction Fund led by my predecessor Ed Husic, a new statement of expectations lifts ambition, clarifies the investment approach and builds momentum around the fund's pipeline of investments. We are allocating $5 billion of the National Reconstruction Fund's capital to the Net Zero Fund to support investment in Australian industry and firms' shift to lower carbon intensity and higher efficiency industrial processes. We are aligning the department's work with the broader package of Future Made in Australia tax and production incentives. We are also taking the opportunity presented by the strategic examination of research and development to work across the CSIRO, university, Defence and public research capabilities and with our private sector research and development system to better align our science and research and development systems to deliver more impact, more commercialisation of Australian inventions and intellectual property here and meet key natural challenges.

Finally, we want to make sure that Australia captures the opportunities of artificial intelligence. We want to share the benefits widely across the economy, including with workers and small business, and keep Australians safe as the technology evolves and new risks emerge. I look forward to the questions today and the discussions over coming months and years about our work meeting these important national challenges. Thank you.
