Senator HUME: Right. So the recruitment company does the due diligence for the original eight, but the department does the due diligence for the ninth board member. But the ANAO said that wasn't documented?

Ms Quinn : That's right. We weren't able to find the due diligence processes. But the interview with the individual who undertook it identified what they had done and the information provided. We could not find in our records the record of the note for file, for example, that identified that. But the individual responsible has provided information to the ANAO.

Senator HUME: I imagine when NGS do a due diligence check that there is some sort of documentation at the end of it. Is it unusual that there would be no documentation if the department would do it?

Ms Quinn : Normally, we would have a record of it through a note for file et cetera. Advice was provided to the minister that identified that had been undertaken and nothing had been found in the due diligence process.

Senator HUME: Advice was provided to the minister but there was no record of documentation that fed into that advice?

Ms Quinn : That's right. There was a process step missed in the department in terms of the note for file to demonstrate what had happened. But the individual concerned has provided that information both to management and to the ANAO.

Senator HUME: Was there any other external executive recruiter engaged to undertake due diligence checks on Mr Thompson, or was it just the department?

Ms Pickworth : Senator, as I mentioned earlier, NGS Global were involved in the original establishment of the board. Subsequent board appointments have been done within our department and in conjunction with our colleagues in the Department of Finance, who then put advice up to the responsible ministers. In addition to what the secretary mentioned, the other part of the NRF board appointments is that we're looking at suitability assessed against the requirements of the act. That's part of what we're looking for when we're doing that work as well. So it's for this appointment for this role. As with any other appointment process, it's looking at suitability for the role. That was undertaken in providing advice through to then ministers responsible for the NRF.

Senator HUME: Why was an external executive search process undertaken for the initial eight board members but not for Mr Thompson?

Ms Pickworth : When we were establishing the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation, we were obviously establishing the board as part of that. NGS Global was used to do that initial search for the board. For subsequent board appointments, we've not used external recruitment companies.

Senator HUME: It was pretty soon after the original eight were appointed though, wasn't it?

Ms Pickworth : From memory, it was October.

Ms Quinn : About a month later.

Ms Pickworth : I think the first board meeting was in September and the subsequent appointment was made in October, from memory.

Senator HUME: So why wasn't Mr Thompson included in the original cohort?

Ms Pickworth : Senator, I think in previous discussions at this committee we've said that it's normal for governments to consider board appointments. That includes looking at making sure there's good coverage in each board. That was part of the normal processes that you would expect with appointments for board members. I note that there has been a subsequent board appointment with one of the original board members stepping down from their role. A similar process was undertaken in appointing the replacement board member there as well.

Senator HUME: When an executive recruitment firm, an independent firm or whoever it might be, is putting together a board and making recommendations to government, they put together a skills matrix. They make sure that they've got somebody who fills every gap. What gap was not filled?

Ms Pickworth : I will go back to the NGS Global part of this. That was an input that was provided through to our department and the Department of Finance to underpin the advice to then ministers. It is very in line with usual processes. Appointments are made, and people step on and off boards. This was all in line in those usual processes.

Senator HUME: But the secretary just admitted that a process step was missed here, so it wasn't in line with your processes.

Ms Quinn : That was a step within the department, not a step in terms of the government consideration of the discussions. As I mentioned, the usual processes were undertaken. The step missing is a recordkeeping step. That was within the department. In terms of the advice provided to the government, the usual processes were followed. Whether we use an external recruitment agent or use internal resources depends on resource constraints at the time. Increasingly over time we do more appointment processes within the department of resources rather than use external consultants. It is consistent with the requirement of the government. It is a core activity to make appointments to boards. We have moved to use public servants and internal processes rather than external consultation processes.

Senator HUME: But it just sounds very strange that one month you needed the external services because of time constraints or whatever it was and then suddenly a month later, after all those board appointments had been made, you decided to use internal processes and then didn't document them.

Ms Pickworth : The NGS Global search was undertaken to inform advice to government around the original board establishment. It was one input into that process. That process went through usual government decision-making processes. From memory, that was some period before September. It was part of the process that led to that board being announced. The first board meeting was held in September, from memory. The subsequent appointments were beyond that. I can see what information we have about the timeframes through that year ahead of the first board appointment in September. I want to make the point that NGS Global was used earlier in that year and that then informed the usual government considerations of a board. Obviously it is a significant appointment process. There was a fair bit of work done through that year around the board appointment process.

Senator HUME: If you could, that would be very good. Obviously, the ANAO has required this information from you, so it should be readily available. I realise my time is up, but I will be coming back to this.

Senator McDONALD: Good morning. I want to refer to FOI300003 that I submitted requesting Minister King's incoming government brief. I submitted this request on 15 May, yet it was not returned to me until 21 August. Can you please explain what took the department so long to find the brief?

Ms Quinn : It's not so much about finding the brief, Senator. It is the processes required under the act for an independent decision to be taken on the request. There are various steps that we're required to do, including consultation with external parties and the like. We went through those processes. We do them for all FOI requests.

Senator McDONALD: Could you identify for me the areas of the brief that required third-party consultation?

Ms Quinn : I'm happy to take that on notice. I don't have that information off the top of my head.

Senator McDONALD: Take that on notice, please. Was consultation with other departments required?

Ms Quinn : I wasn't the decision-maker on this task. I will ask my colleague if she has further information.

Ms Dowdell : Senator, I understand that there was, as part of the normal consultation with departments where there was crossover of responsibilities for their portfolio. Where we might have policy issues that are led by more than our department, we consult with them. I have some further information on the timing.

Senator McDONALD: Terrific.

Ms Dowdell : I think, as was set out in the decision-making letter, there was an extension we requested on 10 June. There was a period of time following that where it was in relation to the payment of charges. So the time frame covered both the search and then the discussions around calculating charges and then the payment of charges, which is why the time frame was that it was then disclosed in August.

Senator McDONALD: On notice, could you please advise me what parts of the brief required consultation with other departments, please?

Ms Dowdell : We can take that on notice.

Senator McDONALD: Thank you for reminding me about the $302.50 that I was required to pay for access to the brief. Do you have a breakdown of what that charge was for?

Ms Dowdell : I don't have the details with me. We'll have to take that on notice. It would be in relation to the number of pages identified and that needed to be provided. That is how that is calculated.

Senator McDONALD: Photocopying?

Ms Dowdell : Search and consideration.

Ms Quinn : Yes. The act sets out what charges are available to departments to apply. It goes to the number of documents, number of pages, decision-making time and timing of the decision-makers et cetera. There's a standard formula that is calculated and used by all those who are subject to the FOI Act. We apply that consistent with the legislation.

Senator McDONALD: Is there a precedent as to the department charging for access to an incoming government brief for the relevant opposition shadow minister?

Ms Quinn : I'm happy to take that on notice. As a default, we apply charges to most of our FOI requests. They do draw on the departmental resources. The act allows us to apply charges.

Senator McDONALD: I appreciate that it may. In the interests of good government and transparency, I don't recall being charged at the beginning of the previous term. I am interested if this is a new element of this government that you are now charging for things that were previously considered part of the democratic process.

Ms Quinn : It's not a governmental decision. It's a departmental decision.

Senator McDONALD: A change in the department's approach to democracy?

Ms Quinn : Given the volume of FOI requests that have increased substantially and the draw on our—

Senator McDONALD: It's because the department and the government is so lacking in transparency that we are now forced to make FOI claims.

Ms Quinn : FOI requests of the department have increased across the board.

Senator McDONALD: Indeed they have.

Ms Quinn : As part of our ongoing stewardship of the Public Service and requirements under the PGPA Act, we have taken a stance to examine fees and charges where we are able to do so. We increased the use of FOI charges through the last parliament.

Senator McDONALD: Perhaps if the department and the government were more transparent, you would save yourself some time and effort. It's just a suggestion. Is there any precedent for the department charging for access to an incoming government brief for any federal politician?

Ms Quinn : I'm happy to take on notice what has been the case for the department in the past. I have already taken that on notice. I'm happy to extend it to parliamentarians.

Senator McDONALD: So you are telling me that this was not the minister's or her office's decision to charge me? It was the department's decision to charge the incoming shadow minister for the brief?

Ms Quinn : The act requires independent decision-making on each application. It is the decision-maker's decision about charges and the application of charges. We have had a discussion in the department about our stance. But there's still individual decision-making at each point. It was the decision-maker's decision in this case, as in all FOIs, as to whether the application of the legislated ability to charge was applied.

Senator McDONALD: I appreciate that. Perhaps you will review your policy on that going forward.

Ms Quinn : We do review it regularly depending on the demands of the department.

Senator McDONALD: Specifically on incoming government briefs. This is a normal process of government. We surely don't want to set a precedent, if it is, as I believe it is, that is going to make it increasingly expensive for shadow ministers, who are incredibly under-resourced under this government, to do their jobs.

Ms Quinn : We review our policies and procedures on a regular basis. We can take that into account.

Senator McDONALD: Thank you. I would like to turn to the roundtables Minister King has been conducting since the election. How many roundtables has the minister conducted?

Ms Quinn : 'Roundtables' is a technical term whose definition is squishy. She did hold some roundtables specifically in the lead-up to the discussion about the roundtables the Treasurer held. She had three of those—one on general resources, one on critical minerals and one specifically with the unions.

Senator McDONALD: Let's go with that as the framework.

Ms Quinn : We do regularly have other industry discussions. Sometimes they are called roundtables. Sometimes they are called forums. It's a regular part of our activity to bring industry together to discuss policy issues and topics. There's no official definition of a roundtable.

Senator McDONALD: Sure. Can you tell me where the location of the three identified productivity roundtables was?

Ms Dowdell : Senator, the resources and critical minerals roundtables were held at the Commonwealth Parliament Offices in Perth. The meeting with the unions was held in the NOPSEMA office in Perth.

Senator McDONALD: Were they catered?

Ms Dowdell : The resources and critical minerals roundtables had a light refreshment provided for participants.

Senator McDONALD: So no catering for the unions and catering for the two for industry. That's a comment. Can the bill be split by food and beverage costs?

Ms Dowdell : Yes. I can take that on notice. It was sandwiches. I think if there was any beverage, it was some juices.

Senator McDONALD: Thank you. Was there a focus for the roundtables? You did say critical minerals. Was gas or economic reform a focus? Can you tell me what the agenda was?

Ms Quinn : The topics across all roundtables were similar. The participants were different. The critical minerals one had parties with a particular interest in critical minerals. Obviously some of those cross over to resources. Minister King was asking the industry for their opinions and views on productivity reform and other economic reforms that they were interested in. It covered a very wide range from the general application of artificial intelligence through to environmental protection and biodiversity changes, energy costs and gas reform. All those sorts of things came up, as you would expect.

Senator McDONALD: To what extent was Minister King involved in the Treasurer's productivity roundtable?

Ms Quinn : The information gathered from the resources, critical minerals and unions roundtables was provided through to the process as were direct requests from regulators in this portfolio, including NOPSEMA. Minister King provided input, as did other ministers, to the process.

CHAIR: I will need to rotate the call.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: I'm interested in what is being done to progress the 12-month consultation the government did on mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings?

Ms Quinn : I don't have officials for that topic here. That is in science and technology.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: I can wait for that.

Ms Quinn : At a very high level, we undertook consultation processes and received submissions. We have assessed those submissions and worked through and provided advice to government. It's with the government.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Is that still work that is in preparation for a national AI safety centre?

Ms Quinn : The government has indicated that it's working on an artificial intelligence capability plan. That information will work towards that outcome.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Minister, is there no plan for a national AI safety centre?

Senator Ayres: You've caught us mid-step, Senator Pocock. The government is working through the capability plan that the secretary has just referred to. We've indicated publicly that we will set that out and have more to say before the end of this year. As a cabinet style government, we are working our way through those questions. As you would appreciate, while of course I as minister and the department have responsibility in terms of the artificial intelligence questions, it is a set of issues that traverses almost every part of government. It's hard to think of a portfolio minister who doesn't have some responsibility or equity in this process. We are working that through, and we'll have more to say later in the year.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: I'm concerned about the pace of this. Your government is in its fourth year. I understand that you are a new minister in this portfolio. I'm hearing that the capability of some of these AI models is doubling every six months, yet six months comes and goes and we don't see any meaningful progress on guardrails.

Senator Ayres: We'll definitely be having more discussion about this. When I say more discussion, I mean later on this afternoon when the relevant officials are here. We are committed to a process here of having clarity on our settings broadly across the economy on artificial intelligence but also in terms of how we approach some of these issues around how the technology evolves and emerges. It's a jagged edge frontier, really. There is sometimes fast progress. It is sometimes a bit slower than some of the boosters predicted it will go. We are working through a thorough process to make sure that we've got a coherent and effective position on all of these questions. We are trying to have not just a drip feed approach, where one bit comes out after another, but a package that gives the sector and Australians some clarity about how this is proceeding.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Thank you, Minister. One of the things I've been hearing is the urgency for guardrails. Indeed, I've heard people in government talking about guardrails for a long time now. I assumed this was something that had been through a process and was essentially ready to be implemented. Are you still consulting on guardrails? Where is the guardrails process up to?

Senator Ayres: As I indicated, I'm a bit restrained in what I can contribute on this question while we're working through a process.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Can you give us an indication of where you're up to in that process?

Senator Ayres: We are closer today than we were yesterday, Senator Pocock. We're intending to deliver that capability plan before the end of the year.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Okay. Minister, as a new minister, have you received your charter letter?

Senator Ayres: Yes.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Great.

Senator Ayres: There are a lot of letters flying around, Senator Pocock.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: I understand that. What about the assistant minister? Has Dr Charlton received his charter letter yet?

Senator Ayres: We haven't provided a charter letter as yet. He is a very busy minister engaging right across the portfolio. I'm very grateful to have the opportunity to work with him. He is going to play a crucial role delivering the government's agenda across the portfolio.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: It does surprise me that, five months in, the assistant minister doesn't have a charter letter. My understanding, doing some research on what that means, is that it actually constrains the assistant minister's authority to act. I understand that he is busy, but he is surely not too busy to receive that letter.

Senator Ayres: I don't think he is constrained in any way really, Senator Pocock. He is full of beans. We engage very regularly. He is deployed across the portfolio, particularly recently in the areas that we've just been traversing. He is playing—and I expect him to continue to play—a very strong role. I'm delighted to have him there. He is a good contributor with a depth of experience and an aptitude for this area of economic, industrial and technology policy. I'm very enthusiastic about the work that we're going to do together.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Minister, I understand that he certainly seems incredibly talented. That for me raises even more concerns.

Senator Ayres: Let's not boost him too much. I've been really nice about him. Let's—

Senator DAVID POCOCK: For me that raises even more questions. You are saying that he is able and he's doing a huge amount. Under our Westminster system he doesn't even have his charter letter yet. Under what authority is he—

Senator Ayres: I don't think it has the impact that you're apprehending. I've operated in an environment as an assistant minister with and without that. It's something that we'll do in due course. It will evolve over time. I'm very confident about the role that he's playing and going to continue to play.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: So you're not concerned about the convention of having ministers and assistant ministers receiving charter letters providing them with authority?

Senator Ayres: We'll work our way through.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: That's something that just happens when it happens, and the Australian public can just—

Senator Ayres: I am working with him very closely. It is a very regular engagement. He is engaged in a lot of work in the portfolio and, of course, in his role as cabinet secretary. Of course, as you pointed out, having recently arrived in the portfolio, I'm taking my time to deliver that in a way that doesn't unduly restrict his capacity to work across the portfolio. There are lots of things to worry about. I don't worry about Assistant Minister Charlton's role here. He has played a very good role.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: I guess as a backbencher I would hope that the government worries more about getting those processes in place, given our system provides that authority. I will move on with the last two minutes. I'm interested in what work is being done to fulfil Australia's obligations under the Bletchley Declaration that we signed back in 2023.

Ms Quinn : As I mentioned, the officials that have the details on that will be appearing later today.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Sure. I'll come back.

Ms Quinn : At a high level, Australian officials are working with other officials under a network of AI safety institutes. We are working with colleagues in other countries sharing information. We've commissioned work from Australian academics to contribute to that process as well. Some of it has been published. As you said before, artificial intelligence models are advancing. The safety institute network was one of the outcomes not just of the Bletchley but also the Seoul process. We are connected into that process. We're working with our colleagues, as you would expect us to.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: How many people in the department are working on AI safety?

Ms Quinn : I'm happy to take that on notice and come back when my officials are here.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Could you take it on notice before they arrive. I think I've run out of time now. Could you provide the FTE and head count of those who are specifically working on AI safety.

Ms Quinn : We will see what we can do. The way we have structured our teams is that we have people working on AI policy, some of which is safety. Some of it is security. Some of it is the opportunities. The most important thing is understanding the technology and then the policy frameworks. We don't have them specifically tagged. We use the technical skills with the policy skills to join things together. I don't know that we can give you a breakdown specifically on safety because that will shift from week to week depending on what is happening. We also have the national AI centre, which is mostly providing information and working with industry and small business. We have technical people and policy people who work across it. I can give you an AI number, but specifically AI safety is a little harder to be precise on.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: I am happy with the AI number, but then maybe you could provide specifically people who have either qualifications or experience directly related to AI safety, please.

Ms Quinn : I'm happy to take it on notice.

Senator HUME: There was a comment before about an additional board member who has subsequently been appointed because one of the original eight dropped away, resigned or was stood down.

Ms Quinn : Yes. Correct.

Senator HUME: That was done through this process that was obviously outside the NGS Global procedures. It was done in a similar way to Mr Thompson. Is that correct?

Ms Quinn : It was done with the Department of Finance's and the department of industry's advice to ministers and then through the usual cabinet process for significant appointments. We would have done exactly the same sort of process of scanning, using all the available information we have, the skills requirements, people's availability and the like, conflicts of interest and all the rest. We did not use an external service for that appointment either.

Senator HUME: Are there documents available that demonstrate that better due diligence was done for that candidate?

Ms Quinn : Yes.

Senator HUME: But not for Mr Thompson?

Ms Quinn : Correct.

Senator HUME: The department told the ANAO that the due diligence check done on Mr Thompson was undertaken in—and I'm using their words—compressed timeframes. Why were the timeframes compressed?

Ms Quinn : The timelines will depend on the sequence and timing of subsequent decision-making. From recollection, it was a requirement to ensure we met deadlines for cabinet consideration.

Senator HUME: Were they deadlines set by you, Ms Quinn? Were they deadlines set by the minister's office? Where did the deadlines come from?

Ms Quinn : It would have been for us to meet the deadlines required of cabinet consideration, which have timelines and the like. It would have been a request from the minister's office probably. They wanted to target the delivery of information to a particular cabinet timing. That's usually how things work. There's a standard set of requirements from our cabinet coordination colleagues about how much information and time to be able to meet cabinet processes. We would have tried to meet those deadlines.

Senator HUME: Is the reason the documentation for the due diligence doesn't exist because it was a rushed process?

Ms Quinn : I would say that it's more to do with a misstep in our internal processes in terms of recording the note for file. That's more to do with the individual circumstances of the people involved in the process.

Senator HUME: The ANAO also said that the department did not document the due diligence checks, that it was all verbal. That is unusual. Why was it all verbal?

Ms Quinn : You have to go back to the individuals running the process at the time. They made decisions to do it in a certain way. Our standard processes are to record it for normal standard processes. From time to time, processes are not met.

Senator HUME: You just said that the individuals made a decision to conduct this a certain way. Did nobody in the department go, 'Hey, this is not quite right. This doesn't feel right?' Were any concerns raised?

Ms Quinn : We have processes and timelines and steps that we ask people to follow. It is not unusual in a department of more than 3,000 people that from time to time some of those steps are missed.

Senator HUME: The original eight board members were taken to cabinet. They were a cabinet decision. The ninth, Mr Thompson, was also a decision taken by cabinet. Is that correct?

Ms Quinn : Yes.

Senator HUME: How would you describe, Ms Quinn, the process to check on Mr Thompson, considering all the things we've just spoken about?

Ms Quinn : My understanding is the usual processes were followed. All the steps that were required were done.

Senator HUME: So it wasn't unusual?

Ms Quinn : All the steps required of a cabinet process were done. All the paperwork, all the checks and all the information required by decision-makers were available to decision-makers.

Senator HUME: Hang on. You just said all the paperwork was available. Clearly it wasn't available because the ANAO said, 'Where was the paperwork?'

Ms Quinn : All the paperwork required for cabinet was available at the time of cabinet.

Senator HUME: Hang on. That just means that all the cabinet submissions were ready to go.

Ms Quinn : All the information required in the cabinet submission, which is around the education requirements, the conflicts of interest and how the appointment meets the legislative requirements. The cabinet handbook sets out the information required for significant decisions. All of that information was available at the time cabinet met.

Senator HUME: I would assume that the cabinet submission said, 'Has all the appropriate due diligence been done?' Somebody says yes—check, tick.

Ms Quinn : And there are also additional requirements in terms of formal CVs and conflicts of interest. There's a sequence of paperwork that is required for all appointments made by cabinet and all other appointments made by ministers or departmental appointments. All of that was done. The step that was missed in the process was a recording of the due diligence at the time the advice was provided to the minister.

Senator HUME: Minister, having heard this evidence from your own officials, that Mr Thompson was appointed to the board which oversees $15 billion worth of taxpayer funds and that this process was seen as inadequate by the ANAO, what would you like to say? Do you have comment on that?

Senator Ayres: I will make two comments. Firstly, you've heard the evidence from the secretary and Ms Pickworth about the steps undertaken here. Actually, I don't agree with your opening comment about how one should approach the Australian National Audit Office. I actually think the process of good government involves being very open with the ANAO, welcoming their intervention and doing the iterative process that goes on. I've observed this for a while now. I haven't been around the joint as long as you. I have been in and out of government on different sides of the estimates table. I have been engaged from opposition on ANAO reports that were critical of the previous government. My observation is that the right culture is welcoming that process. As the secretary has indicated, they have been very precise about what has been recommended here by the ANAO, which is that the process within the department was adequate. There's a step about how the—I have forgotten the term—desktop diligence was documented. The department has engaged with that. It gives me real confidence that the culture is right within the department in terms of the way they engage with those sorts of approaches. They don't have a glass jaw about it. They are listening to it. It's in no way a fatal observation. It's a helpful observation.

Secondly, I'm very confident about this board, its leadership, the CEO, the management and the investment capability that it is developing. As you say, it is $15 billion that gets capitalised over time. They will be here to give evidence later today. I have been very engaged with the management and leadership of the organisation. I've met with the board once. I'm meeting with them again shortly. I've issued a statement of expectations. They are responding to it very well. I'm very enthusiastic about the work that this organisation has in front of it.

Senator HUME: Is Mr Thompson a mate of yours?

Senator Ayres: He is well known to me. He is somebody I worked with in my previous role. It's well-known across the manufacturing sector and government. In fact, he was well known in the previous government, too.

Senator HUME: You mentioned him in your maiden speech.

Senator Ayres: I'll come to that; don't worry. There's a brotherhood and sisterhood of previous industry ministers. I was talking to one of them in the previous government who appointed Mr Thompson to a board and was very engaged with him on matters of policy that went to rail and defence capability in Australia. He is a very experienced, well-regarded—

Senator HUME: You were in the same union together.

Senator Ayres: figure in Australian manufacturing. It wouldn't come as a surprise to anybody really that he is going to play a good role on this board. He is not the only figure with a trade union background. The board is a very well balanced board with all sorts of capabilities across venture capital and emerging technology, the trade union movement and board experience more broadly. I'm very confident about how this board and each of its members is going to engage with the challenges. Of course, I've known Mr Thompson for quite some time. As you say, I worked with him. As you indicated before—top marks for research—I haven't been shy about that. I have indicated that to him along with a series of other officials in that union that I worked with over many years. I have a very high regard for his capability.

Senator HUME: I have two more questions, Chair. Minister, did you discuss Mr Thompson joining the board of the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation with Minister Husic or with Minister Husic's office prior to Mr Thompson's appointment?

Senator Ayres: There are two answers to that. I suppose one is—

Senator HUME: One's the truth.

Senator Ayres: They are both the truth. We're not that late in the night where people start to accuse each other of misrepresenting their position. The first is that I actually just don't recall. The second is that one of the things about being an assistant minister is that you don't get to go to cabinet. Your work is directed really by the senior minister, but you're bound by the same obligations in your role as assistant.

Senator HUME: Do you think Mr Husic knew that he was a mate of yours?

Senator Ayres: Did Mr Husic know? I'm very confident that it is well known to anybody who has even the most passing engagement with the labour movement, the Labor Party or the trade union movement that I and Mr Thompson emerged from the same trade union background. I think it wasn't a surprise to former Senator Hughes when she was asking me the same questions or anybody else. It's not—

Senator HUME: Did you lobby Mr Husic, Minister Gallagher or the Prime Minister about the appointment of Mr Thompson to this very prestigious position?

Senator Ayres: As I indicated, it's a cabinet appointment process. The process has been outlined in terms of the department's engagement with this. It's a cabinet process.

Senator HUME: If he was so qualified, why weren't the same processes followed for Mr Thompson as they were for the eight others?

Senator Ayres: Well, it's a cabinet process. I'm restrained from engaging with the committee for that reason. It was an appointment that was taken to cabinet.

Senator HUME: When did you find out that this appointment was being taken to cabinet? After the decision was made or before?

Senator Ayres: As an assistant minister, I don't have access to the cabinet processes.

Senator HUME: Did you know that Mr Thompson was being considered for this appointment before the cabinet decision was made?

Senator Ayres: I think the engagements and discussions between ministers and the government around appointments is a cabinet process.

Senator HUME: You say it has nothing to do with you. You are saying that it potentially was something to do with you.

Senator Ayres: What I'm saying is that it's a cabinet process. I think he is a very fine appointment.

Senator HUME: I'm not doubting his qualifications. I'm doubting the process that put him there and why he wasn't there in the first place.

Senator Ayres: He's a very fine appointment.

Senator HUME: He was a subsequent appointment and he's a mate of yours. It just doesn't smell right. All the due diligence has disappeared. The ANAO has said this is inadequate. This just sounds like jobs for mates.

CHAIR: Senator Hume, we have to rotate the call because we are running quite over time.

CHAIR: The committee welcomes representatives from the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation. Would you like to make an opening statement? If so, if it could be as brief as possible to help us with time management, that would be much appreciated.

Mr Gall: Certainly, Senator. Thank you for the opportunity to be here today. I would like to make a short statement. I begin by acknowledging the Ngunnawal people, the traditional owners of the land on which we meet today. I'd like to pay my respects to their elders past, present and emerging.

It's almost nine months since I began my tenure as the CEO of the NRFC and more than six months since I last appeared before this committee. These months have been a period of really intense activity but significant progress and growing impact for the NRFC, and I'm pleased to appear before you today to discuss the important matters relating to the fund and how we're executing on our ambitious mandate and our critical purpose. If 2024 was regarded as a period of laying important groundwork, 2025 is the year that we've hit the ground running.

We began making investments in November of last year and, since that point, have made 12 commitments to invest $670 million in companies, businesses and projects that are set to deliver significant impact for Australia and its people. Our investment target for the 2025 financial year was $550 million, and I'm pleased to say that we met and exceeded this target, delivering $584 million in investment. Our investment activities continue to accelerate and expand, in line with our target of investing an additional $1½ billion across priority areas of the Australian economy by the end of the 2025-26 financial year. It's a target we have chosen and we believe is ambitious but achievable.

I want to highlight the commitment and the great work done by the entire staff, particularly our investments team, for getting us to this point. In short time, we've built an impressive, capable team around our chief investment officer, Dr Mary Manning, who is beside me, and the investment specialists we have added to our team. That's allowed us to deliver on our mandate and deliver investments for the Australian people across the seven priority areas of the economy.

Having come to this role after spending decades in the private sector, I can say I've been hugely impressed by the calibre of people we've been able to attract to work at the NRFC and the level of commitment our people display towards the mission and purpose of the fund, which is to transform and diversify Australia's industrial capability. We understand the urgency of the task, and we're committed to meeting the moment. The seven priority areas that have been provided to us in the investment mandate have been well chosen. One of the things that I'm really pleased about is the way our emerging portfolio is already starting to show a good spread of investments across these areas, as well as a strong geographic spread.

We're committed to being a fund for all of Australia, and that is reflected in the investments we've already made. These range from critical minerals opportunities, like our commitment to the Northern Territory's Nolans project, put forward by Arafura Rare Earths, or the Kathleen Valley lithium project of WA's Liontown Resources, to backing world-leading mine safety automation equipment via Queensland's Russell Mineral Equipment. They include investing in quantum computing, information security and semiconductor leaders in New South Wales and the ACT. We've supported satellite and space capability via our investment in South Australia's Myriota, as well as backing medical science deals like our investment in Victoria's PolyActiva and our $200 million investment in Brandon Capital's BB6 fund.

In line with our mandate, these investments are helping to create highly skilled jobs, build Australia's industrial capability, strengthen our national security and contribute to Australia's net zero transition. Most importantly, they will nurture Australia's innovation so that we can stay, grow and scale in this country. If looking back provides a sense of pride, looking forward is a reason for excitement. Over the past 12 months, we've not just built an investment capability; we've built an ability to effectively engage across the investment ecosystem, particularly around manufacturing and innovation. That involves working closely with our specialist investment vehicles and organisations like the Net Zero Economy Agency to ensure that our activities are complementary and collaborative.

It also involves making ourselves more accessible and approachable for Australian companies who want to know more about us and whether or not we can support them. Having come from the banking industry, where there's always a strong focus on delivering for the customer, this has been a particular focus for my leadership. We will not be able to invest in every opportunity that comes our way, but I do want us to be able to deliver a positive experience for all those who engage with us, and we have made some significant strides in delivering on that.

Our ability to identify and build relationships with key stakeholders has increased, and the results have seen a very strong pipeline, with great investments representing all priority areas in states and territories. Now, we've worked hard during recent months to accelerate investment activity while fine tuning the build-out of governance and other processes that a young organisation such as ours needs to operate successfully for the long term. I'm confident and optimistic that the work we've done leaves us in an excellent position to continue expanding and accelerating our activities and our impact as we deliver for the Australian people. We thank you for your interest and welcome the committee's questions.

The statement read as follows—

I welcome the opportunity to appear before the Committee today.

Since our last appearance in February, NOPSEMA has continued to deliver on its key responsibilities as the independent regulator of offshore safety, environment and well integrity, while also furthering a significant program of digital reform.

This work is being driven through Project CORE, our new digital platform transformation that will overhaul and enhance how titleholders interact with us. CORE will consolidate multiple regulatory processes into a single-touch portal, making it easier for industry to lodge environment plans, safety cases and compliance reports, while giving NOPSEMA better visibility of data and trends.

We have recently begun important stakeholder engagement to help inform the platform design. The feedback we receive will be essential to ensure CORE supports both regulatory excellence and industry efficiency. Once in place, Project CORE will foster widespread productivity gains across the entire breadth of NOPSEMA's engagement with titleholders.

Alongside this transformation, we have implemented the recent safety and other measures amendments to the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Act, which came into force in June this year. We have provided updated guidance and held information sessions to help industry understand and meet their obligations under the new requirements.

In 2025 so far, NOPSEMA has accepted 21 environment plans, 63 safety cases and 42 well operations management plans. In the first half of 2025, we conducted 82 offshore inspections. We also have 23 environment plans under assessment.

In addition to these activities, we have seen increased activity in offshore decommissioning. Our compliance and inspection programs are increasingly focused on ensuring decommissioning is conducted safely and responsibly. Importantly, our key performance indicators show improvements since the introduction of NOPSEMA's Decommissioning Compliance Strategy, demonstrating that industry performance in this area is lifting.

We are also guided by our five National Priorities—structural integrity, addressing redundant wells, psychosocial health, control of work and finally, leadership and management. These priorities have been determined based on risk and evidence and they are central in focusing our compliance and enforcement activities. In 2024-25, this has led to targeted regulatory action across environment, safety and well integrity, including the issuing of Improvement Notices, Directions and Prohibition Notices where required.

Another way we are working to foster positive change is through industry education, such as our Better Practice Forums. We received positive feedback on our last forum, "Environmental submissions—collaboration and innovation", which was staged in April 2025.

I want to reassure the Committee that while we modernise how we operate, our day-to-day regulatory performance has not and will not diminish.

Looking forward, our focus is on ensuring that NOPSEMA delivers digital efficiencies for titleholders, strengthens regulatory oversight and ultimately provides confidence to the Australian community through the safe and responsible management of offshore energy resources.

With that, I welcome questions from the Committee.

Chair, Senators—thank you for the opportunity to appear today.

The Net Zero Economy Authority exists because the Parliament asked us to tackle one of the most complex challenges in Australia's history—how we move to a net zero while providing a better future for industrial regions, their communities and workers.

We have three core missions that guide our efforts across the organisation:

1. Help workers in coal and gas facilities affected by the transition to prepare for and find new well paid, safe and secure jobs.

2. Support communities significantly affected by the transition to net zero to prosper, including through economic development and investment.

3. Be a trusted and influential voice to build understanding of, and shape policy on, the regional net zero transition.

Our purpose is to make sure the people and communities who have powered Australia for generations are supported as our energy system evolves.

We are guided by three core principles:

Act where we have levers—delivering programs and frameworks that drive real outcomes.

Partner in regions—working with local leaders, councils, unions, and industry so the solutions are shaped by the people most affected.

Influence nationally—providing trusted advice, aligning policy, and ensuring investment flows where it's needed most.

These are complex problems with no shortcuts. But in less than a year since our establishment in December 2024, we've built the foundation to deliver. We've recruited specialist teams, stood up our core programs, built an evidence base through our Regional Identification Framework, and we're now operating priority regions.

In the Hunter, we've been meeting with workers at the Eraring Power Station ahead of its closure. These communities have been the backbone of Australia's industry for decades Through the Energy Industry Jobs Plan, we're consulting directly with them and their unions to design the support they need: personalised pathways, retraining options, and access to secure, well-paid jobs in the industries emerging around them.

In Central Queensland, the scale is enormous—four coal-fired stations, 24 safeguard facilities, and more than half the State's safeguard emissions. We're working throughout Central Queensland to understand community needs and harness the region's industrial strength.

In Collie, we're walking alongside a community where every household is touched by the closure of its coal mines. The Western Australian Government has made the call to exit coal by 2030. We're working closely with state and local communities to prepare for the closure of Collie Power Station to ensure local workers are supported.

In Latrobe Gippsland, three coal stations—Yallourn, Loy Yang A, and Loy Yang B—together emit more than 38 million tonnes of CO2 each year, 75 percent of Victoria's safeguard emissions. Closers of these power stations will impact the local workers and community. We are here to ensure these closures are well-managed and workers are prepared.

In the Upper Spencer Gulf, where Whyalla, Port Pirie and Port Augusta together produce a third of South Australia's safeguard emissions, we're working with industry and the state on major transformation projects.

And in the Pilbara, one of the world's largest industrial regions, 68 percent of WA's safeguard emissions come from heavy industry. But it's also where over $60 billion in clean energy projects proposed, we are taking a 'project-based' approach to encourage investment in the region, ensuring economic opportunities continue to arise in the Pilbara.

On the delivery front, we've already rolled out the Energy Industry Jobs Plan consultations in the Hunter and Torrens Island, completed the first Regional Identification Framework, initiated investment partnerships with state and international stakeholders, and stood up our corporate systems.

We are only at the start, but we have been in power stations, in town halls, in union rooms, and in council chambers—listening, planning, and acting with the people who've built this country's energy system.

I know that this has been discussed at length at this committee before, and I don't intend to repeat the questions that have already been asked, but I'd like to understand how long this modelling tool has been used and who it was that created it.

Dr Hilton : I could pass that one to Dr Mayfield, but there is a level of detail there.

Dr Mayfield : I can give you a little bit of the answer anyway.

Senator HUME: Yes.

Dr Mayfield : The particular tools that are used in our GenCost work have been around for quite some time.

Senator HUME: When you say 'some time', are we talking three years? Five years? Ten years?

Dr Mayfield : I would argue about 10 years.

Senator HUME: Ten years?

Dr Mayfield : Maybe longer. I can get you an exact answer on that later. They're not new tools, but they do get evolved. There are a series of different models that are used to do that work. The most recent would have been STABLE, which looks at firming costs.

Senator HUME: Stavle?

Dr Mayfield : It is STABLE, s-t-a-b-l-e.

Senator HUME: B! Sorry, it's late in the night.

Dr Mayfield : Yes. It's a submodel that gets used. Overall, there are a number of economic and techno-economic models that get used and that combine together to make the result.

Senator HUME: Are the models put together by a team, by an individual or by a department?

Dr Mayfield : We have a team. We have a techno-economic team, an energy economics team, that sits within our energy research unit.

Senator HUME: A techno-economic team?

Dr Mayfield : Yes. They do quite a range of different studies. GenCost is only one little piece of their workload. They do studies around a whole range of other aspects of energy modelling. They've been doing that for well over a decade.

Senator HUME: The 2024-25 report, on page 23, indicates that people have requested more detail and more information on this modelling. Can you detail for us what types of people or what types of groups have requested this information?

Dr Mayfield : I can't give that to you today, but it will be part of our consultation process. So we can get that for you on notice.

Senator HUME: If you could.

Dr Mayfield : We run a process where we develop a draft report. We then put that out, and we get stakeholder feedback. We run a series of workshops and engagements, which allows them to make comment which we can respond to before we actually produce a final report. We keep a listing of everyone who's made contribution to that, what they've asked about and how we've addressed it. Some of that is captured in the beginning of the report; we talk about some of that response. In terms of a full list, I can get that for you on notice.

Senator HUME: I think would be very interesting to see who it is that's asking for more detail—and not necessarily in order to contribute to it but to, ideally, learn from it and take from it. There are people out there, clearly, who would like to understand how this modelling works, because it does influence so many decisions.

Dr Mayfield : Yes. We get quite a range of different inputs. I think last year, in the last cycle, about 45 different consultation inputs were made formally.

Senator HUME: I hope we're talking about the same thing. I'm not entirely sure we are.

Dr Mayfield : I think we are.

Senator HUME: You're talking about people that are inputting through a consultation process, and I'm talking about people who want to see more data, or see more modelling, and how that works. Is this the same thing, or am I just not speaking techno-economic language?

Dr Mayfield : My belief would be that a subset of the people that provide input have the sorts of questions that you raise. Others make contributions in terms of their industry experience as to certain parameters and operational modes and things like that. It's a mixture.

Dr Hilton: Senator, I think a number of the models are public. Members of the public can access those models, plug in their own data, change assumptions and look at the consequences of different assumptions for the outcomes of the model. One of the things we've really valued with the GenCost report is that level of transparency, both in having contributions and critiques in draft and also in allowing people to access the models themselves.

Senator HUME: Right. My understanding is that the models are not suitable tools for other people to use outside of CSIRO.

Dr Mayfield : There are a couple of different analyses that get done. One is the levelised cost of electricity analysis. As Dr Hilton says, all that data is made available publicly. It's a relatively simple calculation, that one. It is possible to do those independently, and we have provided that information to outside groups.

Senator HUME: Are all of the assumptions that go into that model explicit and transparent?

Dr Mayfield : Yes—all of the parameters that you put in there. That's been one of the points of discussion from the various forums, as to the range of parameters that are chosen. A lot of them come from the AEMO work, but they also come from the consultation process.

Senator HUME: I suppose what I'm trying to get at is that there is some concern that, potentially, the outcomes of the models in the GenCost report aren't verifiable by experts who would like to be able to verify them, because the inputs into those tools are opaque. It's a black box. Because of that, the outcome can't be questioned. How does CSIRO respond to that?

Dr Mayfield : In terms of the levelised cost of electricity, it's very easy to do the calculation. In terms of extrapolating future costs, one of the things that we do is that we get capital costs from Oracle—that's done through a process with AEMO—and then we go through a process to try and estimate what they are as you get greater deployment and things like that. That's a bit more sophisticated. But, again, it's something that you can see; it's not opaque as such.

Senator HUME: If a person much smarter than I will ever be wanted to have a crack and say, 'Let's do some what-if analysis using the GenCost model,' can they do it?

Dr Mayfield : For LCOEs, yes.

Senator HUME: How do they do that?

Dr Mayfield : It's virtually a spreadsheet model.

Senator HUME: I could literally go on to the CSIRO website, and say, 'What if we change the assumptions here or move this about there?' and it could come up with—

Dr Mayfield : You can make changes and assumptions in terms of availability, pricing, rates of return or interest rates and things like that, and you can redo the calculation.

Senator HUME: That's all there?

Dr Hilton : We've walked a number of stakeholders through that process. We're very happy to brief you, your colleagues and the office.

Senator HUME: I won't be doing it myself; it's well above my pay grade. But it's good to know that it's there, and, now that it is on the record that it's there, I'm sure there'll be plenty of people that will have a crack. Maybe I'll come back to you at the next estimates and give you an update on how it went.

Senator Ayres: It's a good offer. The CSIRO's job is to be able to turn these complicated things into language—and conceptually, in a way—that people like us can grapple with. That's part of the plain-speaking science and the industrial application of that, as well as working with people in society and the economies. It's a good offer; you should take it up.

Senator HUME: I couldn't agree with you more. My kids have said, if I don't understand a question, and I need to answer it, I should just say, 'It's science; it's the future. You wouldn't understand the new economy,' and move on. That's what I should say.

Dr Hilton : All our children ever say, Senator.

Senator HUME: I hope to God that's not what CSIRO is saying. I want more than a black box. I want everything to be verified.

Senator Ayres: You'll be right.

Senator HUME: Thank you.

CHAIR: Senator Roberts.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you for being here. My questions are to Professor Sutton. Thank you for attending to clarify the work, Professor Sutton, that CSIRO has been doing. You are director of health and biosecurity at CSIRO, and you have been since September 2023. You lead the Health and Biosecurity Research Unit, which comprises over 350 scientists and focuses on pandemic preparedness, biosecurity and health innovations. My first question is on the CSIRO work on advanced genomics surveillance of influenza strains, including next-generation sequencing to decode thousands of genomes and track mutations in avian influenza. This included studies on viral polymerase activity and host immune evasion. Were these studies of literature, in vitro or using live subjects—rats, for instance?

Dr Hilton : Senator Roberts, the team that is responsible for that is our team at ACDP, which is within Dr Taylor's remit, rather than Professor Sutton's remit. I'd be happy for Dr Taylor to answer that.

Senator ROBERTS: Sure.

Dr Taylor : To clarify your question, you're asking about the sequencing nature of the sequencing experiment?

Senator ROBERTS: Your studies on viral polymerase activity and host immune evasion—were they literature, in vitro or using live subjects like rats?

Dr Taylor : In terms of targeting the virus, I guess that they would—

Dr Hilton : This is influenza virus?

Dr Taylor : Yes. Is this avian influenza virus, Senator?

Senator ROBERTS: I don't know. I just know it's viral polymerase activity.

Dr Hilton : It really depends on which virus. If you can specify the virus, we can tell you a little more about how the experiments are done, because, obviously, different viruses are studied in quite different ways.

Senator ROBERTS: Are any just studied using literature study only?

Dr Hilton : Scientists do literature reviews all the time, and there are large amounts of DNA sequencing information available on public repositories, such as GenBank. Genomicists and bioinformaticians utilise that data as part of their general studies of phylo—

Senator ROBERTS: Including CSIRO?

Dr Hilton : Absolutely.

Senator ROBERTS: Are any done by CSIRO in vitro?

Dr Hilton : It depends on the virus.

Senator ROBERTS: Are any done by in vitro?

Dr Hilton : Are any studies on any viruses done in vitro? Yes.

Senator ROBERTS: What about using live subjects, animals?

Dr Taylor : Yes, I think we do use animal models to study certain viruses. That's correct. But, again, it does depend on which virus.

Senator ROBERTS: Sure. I appreciate that. I'm not technically sufficient and I haven't got the list of viruses with me. What real-world situation benefited from this research? For example, that could be COVID or the recent bird flu outbreak? How is this applied in the real world?

Dr Hilton : One of the things that I'm proudest of, of the work at ACDP, is the important monitoring work they've done with state departments of agriculture around outbreaks of avian influenza, the H7 virus, over the last 18 months. I think the last case was in February. The team at ACDP was on call for much of that time. They were responsible for assisting the state authorities managing those outbreaks in a way that I believe was of immense value to the agricultural sector.

Senator ROBERTS: Using bioinformatics, CSIRO modelled influenza's antigenic drift, predicting evolutionary paths from over a decade of genomic data. Has this research been used in a real-world situation?

Dr Taylor : The example I can think of is that, in our avian influenza work, we do sequence some influenza samples in wild birds, and we know that that's a vector pathway of risk to bring avian influenza H7 into Australia. We monitor the viral load in those wild birds to see if we can get an early detection as to whether something will cross into a poultry farm. Sequencing is used there because we keep a database of the relationship of those sequences and wild birds. If we detect, as we did earlier this year, a H7 outbreak or confirm a H7 outbreak in a poultry farm, we can look at the relationships between those sequences and determine whether that likely came from a wild bird or from somewhere else.

Dr Hilton : There was a profoundly important moment during the outbreak, I think the second outbreak in Victoria, where two farms linked to the same owner, the same farmer, but quite geographically distant, both came down with an avian influenza outbreak. The bioinformatic analysis of the DNA sequence from those two isolates showed that they were, in fact, two different strains that had arisen independently and therefore there was much less likelihood of there having been bird-to-bird spread between the two farms. That was profoundly important in the way the department of agriculture then managed the outbreak. This is a great example of where sophisticated bioinformatic and genomic analysis using DNA sequences generated by the ACDP and comparing it with data online using bioinformatics had a major positive impact for our agricultural sector.

Senator ROBERTS: In 2020, the CSIRO conducted preclinical testing of two candidate vaccines including Oxford–AstraZeneca in animal models like ferrets funded by CEPI. And I note ferrets are mentioned again on your website in 2022 research around Vaxzevria. Was the animal experimentation conducted by the CSIRO or did you use work done elsewhere?

Dr Taylor : Thank you for the question. The animal work done in ferrets was conducted at our Geelong facility, the Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness.

Senator ROBERTS: What happened to the ferrets when CSIRO finished with them?

Dr Taylor : As per normal protocols under our regulations, they were humanely euthanised.

Senator ROBERTS: How many times has the CSIRO used animals for testing over the last five years and how frequently did the CSIRO destroy the subject afterwards?

Dr Hilton : I'll take that on notice.

Senator ROBERTS: Does anyone in the room know the answer?

Dr Hilton : No, that would not be a detail we could give you an accurate answer on. It requires us to go back and look at large numbers of experiments over that five-year period.

Senator ROBERTS: Your website mentions the work you did on the Hendra virus vaccine. I think it is the Zoetis marketed vaccine for Hendra called Equivac. Was the CSIRO involved in the development of Equivac actively or through Zoetis using your work.

Dr Hilton : My understanding is, and, again, I will give you this answer on notice, but my understanding is CSIRO was essential to the management of the initial Hendra outbreaks in Queensland and northern New South Wales and then on the understanding of the virus and the development of the vaccine. But I will give you a detailed answer on notice.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you. How much did you charge Zoetis and are you still involved in Equivac adverse event monitoring?

Dr Hilton : I'll take that question on notice.

Senator ROBERTS: My questions now go to pandemic preparedness. This is the Australian—

Senator Ayres: We're off the horses and ferrets now, Senator Roberts?

Senator ROBERTS: Yes, and the rats and the birds.

CHAIR: Senator Roberts, you've got three minutes.

Senator Ayres: We're now going to move on to the main event.

Senator ROBERTS: The Australian Health Management Plan for Pandemic Influenza was developed over 10 years, concluding in 2019, just in time for COVID. But it wasn't used; it was binned. As your department is pandemic preparedness, Professor Sutton, are you working on updating this plan and correcting whatever reason caused it not to be used?

Dr Hilton : Again, Professor Sutton is not responsible for the ACDP, which is our centre for pandemic preparedness. Professor Sutton is responsible for our research unit, named health and biosecurity.

Senator ROBERTS: Does the CSIRO handle live viruses? Your achievement page mentions lyssavirus—including rabies and Ebola, for example. If you have live viruses, which ones do you have?

Dr Hilton : So are we back to horses and weasels and ferrets?

Senator ROBERTS: Just viruses.

Dr Hilton : Yes; we hold a number of—

Senator ROBERTS: I treat this pretty seriously.

Dr Hilton : So do I.

Senator Ayres: I'm trying, Senator.

Dr Hilton : I just want to make sure we're going back to your first line of questions.

Senator ROBERTS: I'm just going through whether or not you handle live viruses.

Dr Hilton : I think we've established that. We do handle live viruses.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you. Can you assure the committee that CSIRO will not slip up in the way the Wuhan Institute of Virology did in the escape of their Frankenstein COVID experiment?

Dr Hilton : I would not characterise it in that way. CSIRO takes its responsibility for biosecurity exceptionally seriously in all of its facilities and works closely with regulators to ensure that it maintains the highest standards.

Senator ROBERTS: So you can give me an assurance it won't escape?

Dr Hilton : What won't escape?

Senator ROBERTS: Live viruses.

Dr Hilton : Any live viruses? I will give you assurance that we work assiduously to maintain the highest standards of biosecurity as an organisation, across our sites.

Senator ROBERTS: Highest standards—can you give me an assurance that they won't escape?

Dr Hilton : Senator, we maintain our facility to the highest standards of biosecurity.

Senator ROBERTS: Can you give me an assurance it won't escape?

Dr Taylor : Senator, I can add that the Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness is one of three facilities in the world that has the highest biocontainment. It is quite unique in its capabilities. Its box-in-a-box design means that, even if the facility fails and if electricity fails, there are triple redundancies in the system. It is world renowned for its secure capabilities. That is why we handle high consequence live viruses there, and that's its purpose. It's done that for 40 years without a biosecurity breach.

Senator ROBERTS: Obviously you won't give me an ironclad guarantee, but that's fine. In Professor Sutton's podcast interview, conducted recently, he made the statement that the government could consider not introducing the intrusive COVID social restrictions—lockdowns for instance. Is his opinion based on the work you have done at CSIRO or could you expand on what aspects of the social restrictions should be reconsidered? If Professor Sutton can't answer it, perhaps you could do it.

Dr Hilton : I think that would be one that Professor Sutton could shed light on—to the interview.

Senator Ayres: He's been champing at the bit to respond!

Prof. Sutton: That reflection was really based on the fact that it's a matter for future governments as to the policy settings in response to any future pandemic. It's not for me to say what the settings could be, but I could certainly imagine a future in which policy decisions could be less restrictive than we've experienced historically.

Senator ROBERTS: Thank you very much. See, that wasn't so difficult.

Prof. Sutton: Not at all.

Dr Hilton : It was a pleasure.

CHAIR: Thank you for your rapid-fire approach, Senator Roberts.

Senator Ayres: Unbridled enthusiasm.

CHAIR: Senator Pocock, if we could restrict questions to five minutes, I'd highly appreciate it.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Best endeavours, Chair, thank you. I wanted to ask about budget. Table 3.1 on page 114 of the portfolio budget statement shows a $176 million reduction in employee benefits between this financial year and the next. Dr Hilton, I'm interested if you can tell us how many staff positions this will translate to and over what timeframe?

Dr Hilton : I'll pass the detailed financial question to Mr Munyard, our chief operating officer.

Mr Munyard : For future years we're working through our budget planning now, and we've begun our research portfolio review, on which we could go into greater detail for you. In the past financial year we saw a 9.4 per cent reduction of headcount, and so far in the current financial year we've seen a 3.3 per cent reduction in headcount. For last year's reduction—that's a part-year effect—we'll expect the full-year impact of that reduction to come in this year and next, and the same for the reduction we've seen so far this year. So, as I said at the start, at the moment we're working through our budget planning for next year and beyond in order to give a definitive answer in relation to that.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Okay. What proportion of the savings in employee benefits will come from nonrenewal of contracts versus redundancies?

Mr Munyard : Again, we're working through the budget planning for that. We are—

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Maybe for the nine per cent and the three per cent? Do you have that?

Mr Munyard : I don't have the exact split of that. That headcount reduction is 818 in total.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: What saving does that amount to?

Mr Munyard : In terms of labour reduction overall, we would expect that to be around $120 million, I think.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: And you're looking at a further $176 million next financial year?

Mr Munyard : Again, we're anticipating doing our budget planning. But I will say that in the 2024-25 year, starting as a base, there was a redundancy provision including those employee expenses. So, that would have to be removed from that figure as well. That's why I can't give you a definitive answer.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Yes, I understand that there's a lot of work to do, but we're talking about roughly 1,000 employees? I mean, your budget is being reduced by $176 million.

Mr Munyard : It's been reduced by 818 to date, which is a large proportion of that saving to date, and we'll work through the budget planning for the remaining financial years.

Dr Hilton : Senator, perhaps to give you some context: the reduction in labour over the past 18 months has been partly in response to the ending of the COVID safety measure, and the organisation has tackled that in a couple of different ways. The first was that we looked at the non-research part of our business and could see some opportunities for simplification of what we do. And I want to acknowledge the impact that that's had on staff. That is not an easy process.

We also ask our research units to manage their project flow, and that is both appropriation funded projects and projects co-funded with the external revenue. That's also led to some reductions in non-indefinite staff—the term ends, the contract ends. That's just a normal part of project management and the ebb and flow of budgets. We do have some challenging sustainability issues as an organisation. The value of the appropriation has not kept up with the cost of doing science, and we have some legacy property issues that need investment in order that we maintain safe, fit-for-purpose and, where appropriate and possible, cutting-edge facilities.

The ACDP is a good example of that. We're provisioning funds to enable us to begin the renovation of that facility. It celebrates its 40th anniversary this year. That is 10 years past the midlife refit. It's really important that we invest in that national facility, and that really is a microcosm for CSIRO's challenges.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Thank you. Minister, I've had some work done by the parliamentary library and want to table this. Given that per capita investment in the CSIRO is now less than half of what it was in the 1980s and has fallen by 87.5 per cent as a percentage of GDP, how can Australians have confidence that the organisation is properly resourced to meet national science challenges, when we're hearing about these sorts of layoffs, challenges with facilities and declining funding?

Senator Ayres: We've had this discussion a little bit offline, and I think it's fair to say that, while the government asserts that nominal funding hasn't changed over that period, of course you will assert that in real terms that's a different story—and I haven't seen the work of the Parliamentary Library on this question. I do say that there is a very substantial investment from the Commonwealth government into the CSIRO.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Where?

Senator Ayres: It's a substantial annual contribution—

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Declining.

Senator Ayres: to our national science institution. I appreciate your point about the difference between nominal and real contributions, but I say it is a significant contribution to an important national science institution. I expect the management of the CSIRO to work with the staff of the CSIRO to make sure that the organisation is on a sustainable budget footing and that work is going on. Officials have described some of that to you. They'd be very happy to answer further questions. I also want to make sure, as the Minister responsible for science in the Commonwealth government, that the CSIRO is continuing to evolve its approach to make sure its programs of effort are in line with the national science priorities of the country and what the country needs in order to solve the big national challenges in front of us. That is that the challenge of leadership in this organisation. It is not the only place that research is done in Australia. Of course, you know that the Strategic Examination of Research and Development will conclude its work on behalf of the government towards the end of this year. I'm watching closely and working closely with the leadership of the CSIRO on their work. I'm watching closely and working closely with the leadership of the research and development review. And I'm looking forward to making sure that not only do we have a national science institution that is budget sustainable and directed in the right way but also that we've got a national research and development capability—public and private, state and Commonwealth—that serves the country's interests well.

CHAIR: Senator Pocock, we've four minutes until close.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: One more question.

CHAIR: A quick one, and then we'll try and get Senator Whish-Wilson.
